utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber shall now issue its ruling in relation to the accused's request made orally by Mr. Robinson on the 16th of February, 2012, to exclude certain parts of Robert Block's evidence. The evidence sought to be excluded relates to Mr. Block hearing from two different sources that the accused was angry at Zoran Petrovic for releasing Srebrenica-related footage into the public domain and that the accused demanded that this footage be recovered or confiscated. According to Block's statement, the two sources in question were Petrovic himself and an unidentified driver Mr. Block had worked with at the time. The accused argues that this evidence is insufficiently reliable to be admitted because it is at minimum triple hearsay. In addition, he notes that newspaper articles written at the time by Block and another journalist who was present when Petrovic allegedly told Block that was upset made no mention of the accused. Further, the accused notes that the other journalist, when interviewed by the Prosecution, never mentioned the accused in this context and neither did Petrovic-Pirocanac. Finally, in support for his request for exclusion, the accused relies on two Milutinovic decisions in which the Trial Chamber refused to admit certain evidence on hearsay grounds. In response, the Prosecution submits that Robert Block's evidence is sufficiently probative and reliable to be admitted as he spoke directly to Petrovic who then told him that the accused was upset with him. The Prosecution also points to the fact that Petrovic was in direct contact with the accused in 1995 and that the accused publicly expressed negative attitude towards Serbs providing foreign news agencies with footage or pictures related to the conflict. The Chamber has carefully considered the arguments of both parties and has looked at the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence on hearsay evidence as well as the Milutinovic decisions relied upon by the accused. In that respect, the Chamber recalls the well-established Appeals Chamber jurisprudence that hearsay evidence is admissible and that its reliability depends on the circumstances under which it arose, as well as on its content. Having done so, the Chamber has decided to deny the accused's request and allow the Prosecution to lead the evidence in question. The Chamber bases this decision on the fact that this part of Robert Block's evidence is based on his direct interaction with Petrovic and as such is not comparable to the evidence that the Trial Chamber in Milutinovic refused to admit, namely, NGO reports of alleged crimes, based on interviews with identified and unidentified sources and tendered in court through persons who did not conduct those interviews. The Chamber also notes that the fact that Block's evidence may be triple hearsay is something that will go to its weight and is also something that the accused can cross-examine Block on. Having said that, however, the Chamber would prefer to hear this part of Block's evidence live in its entirety. Thus, the Chamber orders the Prosecution to redact the last sentence of paragraph 25, as well as the entire paragraph 26 of Mr. Robert Block's statement and lead the evidence contained therein live. The Chamber also has considered the accused's request that the testimony of Milan Lesic and Ljubomir Obradovic be led live and issues the following oral ruling. In relation to Milan Lesic, the Chamber notes that the voluminous 92 ter evidence sought to be admitted through this witness contains a substantial amount of information about the witness's financial assistance to Republika Srpska leaders after 1995 and about his meetings with the accused and Ratko Mladic in 2001. The Chamber further notes that a large part of the written evidence of this witness pertains to the witness's explanations of photographs and video footage. The Chamber therefore considers that it is in the interests of justice to grant the accused's request that Milan Lesic be led live and orders the Prosecution to focus on the parts of the evidence which are relevant to the indictment. The Chamber further decides that the accused's cross-examination shall not exceed the time taken by the Prosecution for its direct examination. As regards Ljubomir Obradovic, the Chamber will give its ruling during the course of today. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to put on the record before Mr. Block comes in that we continue to object to testimony by war correspondents without the privilege being waived. I have nothing more to say than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the microphone was not on. Could you kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me well, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Robert Jeffrey Block.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: At the moment I'm a company executive with an aerospace company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What were you -- what was your profession prior to becoming a company executive?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: For almost 30 years I was a journalist and for most of that time a foreign correspondent for various news organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you give us a little bit more detail about who you worked for during that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I started out as a reporter for small papers in Florida, which is where I'm originally from. Am I supposed to be hearing something in the mike -- in the earphones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are hearing yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am hearing myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is a bit loud to you. Could the usher assist the witness. Mr. Karadzic, could you say something in B/C/S to check whether the witness can hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all. Good morning to all, and I'd like to say hello to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I hear now. Now I hear myself as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I was saying that first I worked for small papers in Florida, which is where I'm originally from, and then I went on to -- I moved to Mexico City where I secured a job with Reuters News Agency which was based in Britain but was an international news organisation. I spent about almost 10 years there. Then I took a job with "The Independent" newspaper in London first as an assistant foreign editor and then as their chief foreign correspondent, which basically meant I got to go to places other people didn't want to. And then I had a brief stay at "The Sunday Times" of London, and then I joined "The Wall Street Journal" where I was a correspondent first based in Africa and then I roved around again covering central Europe and the Middle East. And then Mr. Murdoch bought the paper and I left and took a job with "The Orlando Sentinel" back -- completing the circle back in Florida covering space and thus my -- leading to my current occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: During your time as the chief foreign correspondent of "The Independent," can you tell us which situations and which conflicts you were covering?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I covered -- I tend to cover some of the most horrific places and I would also do it for long stints of time. I would be based in London but I would be sent out and I would cover the Middle East, especially if something was going wrong, which there was not uncommon. The break-up of the former Yugoslavia. I covered Africa often, the genocide in Rwanda. Basically wherever people were being nasty to each other I would end up being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit specifically about your coverage of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. How did you first come to be aware of that and start reporting on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was after the -- after the first Gulf War. I was writing a book about Palestinians and their experience in Kuwait, and that book -- the publishing house never -- never saw the light of day, and the war in Yugoslavia broke out, and I ended up taking -- leaving book leave and going back to "The Independent" and almost instantly was -- was told to go to Yugoslavia, and I was in Yugoslavia in various places. I mean, I took a rather different -- with the -- with "The Independent" agreeing to the approach that I took, I felt that there were so many people in -- in Sarajevo, which was the focus of a lot of the coverage of the war itself, and then many were in Zagreb looking at the war from the point of view of the UN and humanitarian agencies, that I felt that I should float around everywhere but those places and try to -- to take a look at what wasn't making the headlines and try to shine a light on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: During this time you were covering the conflict, did you go to the area of Eastern Bosnia and Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I think, actually, the first day that I arrived in Belgrade, which I think was the first place that I went there, it was 1993, I believe, and the first place that I heard that there was something to be seen was down along the Drina valley. We drove down past along -- along -- along the river, which it basically defines the border between Serbia and Bosnia, and we went a little past a village at the time called Ljubovija. I think it's still called Ljubovija. And we were able to sit inside of Yugoslavia on the road and watch Muslim soldiers from Bosnia burn a small Serbian village called Bjelovac, and I watched that with people on the side of the road who were from Serbia and a woman from Bjelovac, and we just actually sat there and watched the village destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you speak the Serbo-Croat language?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Enough to get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 4th of September, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you provided a further statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th of November, 2009?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 90314A in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, on the 14th of February, 2012, you signed an amalgamated statement that was a combination of your 1995 and 2009 statements with some additional information that you provided to the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show him the bottom part so that he can see the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that this amalgamated statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of your two earlier statements and the information that you recently provided?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statements, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the statement. There's a public redacted version and an under seal version, because there's a document that is quoted later in the statement at paragraph 41(A) that was supplied under a condition that it not be used or quoted in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit the two versions, and I take it the redaction that was ordered by the Chamber will be done in due course. Yes, we'll give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 90314 will be Exhibit P4392, under seal, and 65 ter number 90314A will be Exhibit P4393.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We also had ten associated exhibits with that statement, and I have requested leave to add five of them to our 65 ter list and then have them admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the addition will be granted. I have two points, Mr. Mitchell. With respect to 65 ter 23615 and 23617 which you were -- dealt with the paragraph you referred to, para-41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That the witness says just -- I believe that -- I can say it in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "I believe that the man I referred to in my article as Resid Halilovic is the same man referred to as Resid Simonovic and Resid Sinanovic respectively in these two documents," but I don't see how he reaches that conclusion. So I would like you to deal with that part live --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- with respect to those documents. Otherwise, the remaining eight documents will be admitted and be given a number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a summary of Mr. Block's statement. On 15 July 1995, Mr. Block arrived in Belgrade to report on the fall of Srebrenica. There, he met a colleague, Dragan Cicic, who told him about a documentary that had been broadcast that day by the Belgrade TV station Studio B. Mr. Cicic said that the documentary contained some amazing footage shot in and around the Srebrenica area. On 16 July, Mr. Block and Mr. Cicic went to Studio B and watched the documentary that had aired the previous day as well as the raw footage from which the documentary had been made. This footage had been videotaped in the Srebrenica area on 13 and 14 July, 1995, by a Serbian journalist called Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac. Among this footage, Mr. Block saw a short clip of what looked like the bodies of 20 to 25 men who appeared to have been killed in an execution. He also saw images of detained men being held on the balcony of a white house and men being led out of the white house at gunpoint. At Studio B that day, Mr. Block also saw video footage taped in Bratunac on 14 July 1995 by a Bosnian Serb television station. This footage showed hundreds of men on a football field forced to stand up and sit down. Mr. Block has never again seen the Petrovic footage of the men leaving the white house under gunpoint, nor the Bosnian Serb TV station footage of the Muslim men on the football field being forced to stand up and sit down. Based on the footage he saw that day at Studio B, Mr. Block wrote an article called "Bodies pile up in horror of Srebrenica," which was published in "The Independent" newspaper on 17 July 1995. On 17 July 1995, Mr. Block returned to the offices of Studio B to find that the footage had been confiscated. After learning that the footage had been confiscated, he set out to find more information. He and Dragan Cicic first tried to get a permit to go to Pale but were told that they would be arrested if they tried. Instead, they drove to Ljubovija. After being denied permission by the Serbian authorities to cross into Bratunac, they instead parked their car next to the Ljubovija-Bratunac bridge and spoke with Serbs who crossed over the bridge from Bratunac. From these people, Mr. Block heard accounts of thousands of Muslim men being executed by the Bosnian Serbs. He recalled one particular woman saying words to the effect of, How do you not know what's going on over there? Everyone knows what's going on. Over the next two days Mr. Block tried to corroborate this information. By the evening of Thursday, the 20th of July, he felt that he had enough corroborating evidence to publish the story and it ran in "The Independent" newspaper on Friday, the 21st of July, 1995, in an article entitled "Mass slaughter in a Bosnian field knee-deep in blood." By this time, Mr. Block concluded that the execution of the Muslim men was no secret on either side of the Drina River in the region of Bratunac and Ljubovija. In the following days, Mr. Block went back to the areas of Bratunac, Ljubovija, and Loznica, where he continued to hear accounts about the execution of thousands of Muslim men. One of the execution sites he heard about was on the bank of the Drina River. Mr. Block went to this area and spoke with people who said they watched from the Serbian side of the Drina River as people were pushed off the back of trucks and shot. They also described seeing earth-moving equipment pushing earth over the bodies. This information was published in "The Independent" newspaper on July 25 1995 in an article by Mr. Block entitled "River killings shed light on scale of horror after the fall of Srebrenica." During this period, Mr. Block also learned of a Muslim lawyer from Srebrenica who was rescued from the Drina River after having been shot several times, then treated at the sanitorium at Banja Koviljaca and the hospital at Loznica before being returned to the RS MUP at Bijeljina. Mr. Block published this information in his 25 July article entitled "River killings shed light on the scale of horror after the fall of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, I have some additional questions about a few different topics. If I can first pick up what the President asked, and if I can actually bring up a copy of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: 65 ter number 90314, the under-seal version. So this shouldn't be broadcast. If we can go to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, if you can have a look at paragraph 41?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing these two documents that were shown to you in a proofing session --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- last week? Now in paragraph 41 of your statement, you say: "I believe that the man referred to in my article," that's your July 25 1995 article, "as Resid Halilovic is the same man who is referred to in the two documents that you were shown." Can you explain what the basis of your belief that this is the same man is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Can I mention the third document, the third bit as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can explain anything --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It was very common while covering the former Yugoslavia that names and numbers were always the most difficult thing to ascertain when they were true or not, and it was not uncommon to hear one man referred to using a nickname and another man, you know, referred to with his full name and it turned out to be the same name. This was a very, very specific event that was described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can I interrupt you. Has the 65 ter 23615 has been published or uploaded? Yes, now I can see it. Yes, Mr. Block, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a very specific event that was described of -- by people who were on the river that day outside of Banja Koviljaca when they saw a man in the river and they went to his rescue. And they brought him to Banja Koviljaca, and then at Banja Koviljaca, after being just tended to lightly, was sent on to Loznica. He was a lawyer. The first name, you know, was Resid. The likelihood of a coincidence between -- there was another document that made -- I believe it was a Bosnian Serb intelligence report talking about a wounded lawyer found in the same area. It just -- it seems patently obvious to me that all three of these reports, the two referred here -- a -- one referred to much more -- in a much sketchier fashion than what I had learned about that day, were the same. The coincidence would be just too close to call to imagine it any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now have 65 ter 13264 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, this is your article of 17 July called "Bodies pile up in horror of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd just like if you can briefly talk us through that experience on 16 July when you were sitting in the studios at Studio B and you see this footage for the first time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: We were brought into -- we were given some video tapes and basically given a brief explanation in how to work the editing equipment on which we were viewing them and we didn't know what order the tapes were in and we saw the documentary which was cut already. And we were coming through it in -- there's a very -- it's a very short sequence in which you see -- obviously it's being filmed -- it appears to be filmed from a car as they were driving by. So you see the camera move across what looked like a -- a wall with two -- a large metal garage door or a large door, and it swings by and it looks at the bottom of the wall that there was clothing there, and I would have not -- I would have let it slide had the voice over the tape not said there were many dead Muslim soldiers. So what we did was we asked them to go back and bring it frame by frame to basically take a look and it slowly dawned, as you go by, that we weren't looking at piles of belongings, we were looking at bodies that were all piled up. And it was -- you know, the -- the -- it wasn't crisp clear, the footage, but it was nonetheless shocking, and at the same time it was very difficult to believe what your eye was seeing. We -- we went back several times, back and forth, over the footage to make sure that this wasn't an illusion or something that your brain was somehow, you know, trying to convince your eyes to see. And sure enough you could see easily it looked like 20 to 25 bodies. There was a man in a white T-shirt in the front. There was another man, I remember, with a dark shirt, and -- and it did not look like any combat scene in 20 years of war corresponding that I had ever seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P4269 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, while we are waiting for that document, you tendered, I take it, 65 ter 23615 and 23617.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't admitted it officially yet. So we will now admit it but shall we put it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Only 23615 needs to be under seal, Mr. President. 23617 doesn't have the same restriction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 23615 will be Exhibit P4402, under seal, and 65 ter 23617 will be Exhibit P4403.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, do you recognise the image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the scene from the documentary that was broadcast on Studio B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to mark a couple of things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you understand this is a composite image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I mean, you know, you would not have been able to see it like this on the screen, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to assist you. You mention in paragraph 3 of your 17 July article the fit body of a young man in the foreground filled out a white T-shirt. Can you circle what it is that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You also describe brown reddish blotches on the wall and dark stains on the garage doors behind the bodies.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: You can't see that as clearly from this as you could from the footage that I had seen. And it was of the -- you saw it on the doors here. And of course, you have bullet holes that I also refer to throughout, and then also on the screen on the footage that I saw, which was a little bit -- you could see more clearly. You could see the bullet holes on the black door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you put a 1 next to the body in the white T-shirt?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then a 2 next to the mark that you put on the doors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just for the record, the markings to the left and to the right of that were, where Mr. Block circled, bullet holes. If you can just initial and put today's date down the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Today's the 21st; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: 21st, correct.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just one more question while we're looking at this. Was the footage you saw that day, on 16 July, was it better quality than this footage from which this composite or this picture was made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first generation because it was the actual documentary. It was probably actually a second generation because it was made from the material that it was taken from, but, yes, it was, and also, I also saw the raw footage. A lot of the scenes that you see in the documentary are actually shorter than the ones on the -- the raw footage that was use, the rushes that were used to -- to edit the documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, after you saw this footage on 16 July and then found out the next day that it had been confiscated, did you take any steps to find out what had happened to this footage?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well -- well, let me take one step back. The minute we saw the footage and wrote about the footage, it was my suspicion, indeed instinct, that it would not stay around for too long. I had made an effort, indeed the night that I had written the story, which was the 16th, to call colleagues of mine in broadcast media, specifically I remember the BBC, telling them what was on this tape and urging them to -- to try to get a copy of it before it disappeared, which I was convinced it would. Indeed the next day they told me that it had. Now, this is a very awkward situation for a journalist to be in. There are two things that foreign correspondents, and particularly people covering conflicts like this where everyone thinks you're a spy or an enemy, is you never want to be last on a story, and you never want to be first on a story without anyone able to come behind you and corroborate what you had been writing. So it was definitely in my interest to make sure that other people saw this, to know that -- you know, people were always accusing us, from every side, of being propagandists or anti-this or anti-that or pro-this or pro-that, and so this was in some ways the only eyewitness footage of what had happened in this area that I was aware of, and it was very important after I saw it that it was available for other people to see to validate my own reporting. So, yes, we tried to figure out what had happened to the tape so we could get it out so it would make my reporting stand up, and we had heard that -- that the -- I think I'd written at the time that Bosnian Serb authorities had had the tape confiscated, and specifically I think that on various -- both occasions there were military -- Bosnian Serb military officials who picked them up. But what I had heard -- now, you have to understand, what happened to the tape was of less concern to me at the same time, because almost immediately after writing the story and trying to get -- figure out where the tape was, we went down to the area and -- Ljubovija, and had heard reports that thousands had been killed, which was an extraordinary number in Yugoslavia. You know, you had had reports of dozens or hundreds that would draw cries of protest, but thousands and the number at the time was up to 4.000, which in a very short period of days was extraordinary. So most of our effort at that time had gone into trying to validate if this was true or a desire to create propaganda. So we were not reporting specifically by this time on what had happened to the tape. There was very little more that I could do than report what was on the tape. It was really up to everyone else, but what I had heard from a friend of mine in Pale, who was an interpreter and driver with whom I had worked for for years and whom I had a close personal relationship with, and what I also heard from Zoran Petrovic, was that the authorities were very angry and that they had understood that the President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic himself, was angry over this footage. Upon hearing this it didn't seem to be out of the realm of possibility, but it was not something I set about corroborating myself for the story. It was tangential to the larger task of determining whether indeed what we had been told that day on the riverside in Ljubovija that thousands had been killed was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you heard this from Zoran Petrovic. Can you tell us a little bit more about the specific circumstances under which you heard that from Zoran Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well -- well, Dragan and I had -- Dragan and I had gone out to see him to basically find out what happened to the tape, and he was clearly not a happy man. He had called previously and was angry that I had even written about the tape and had seen it, because he didn't feel that that was somehow appropriate, and I had the distinct impression during the time that I was talking to him that he was under pressure himself from various people who obviously helped him get access to the footage, who was -- who were not pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when you went and saw Zoran Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It would have been the day after -- the 15th I arrived. That was Saturday. The 16th we reviewed the tape. The 17th we found out it had been confiscated but took off to go to Ljubovija. And the 18th I believe was a Tuesday. We had come back to try to basically determine if -- if other people in Belgrade were hearing similar things and also to speak to Petrovic because obviously the tape starts to take on added significance when people along the river are talking about thousands of men being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can -- I forgot to tender that marked exhibit earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Block, who was Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Cicic was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- a writer for "Nin" and who often acted as -- as a reporting partner of mine and a source of -- he had a tremendous sense of humour and made even the worst situations bearable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit more now about your trip to Ljubovija on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 23519 in e-court, page 10. If I can blow this up and just focus on -- maybe just a little bit more. Just one more click. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can make it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, can you see the Bratunac-Ljubovija bridge on this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to assist you, I'll get you to mark that or to circle it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can put a B next to the town of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And an L next to Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And an X where you and Dragan Cicic parked your car that day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: We parked just south of the bridge. Just -- on the road. Just -- actually I think the trunk of the car was just in the bushes, out of sight of the guards from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more, describe to us those trips that you made that day between the bridge and Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, we had -- Dragan and I -- I drove, and we -- we got a car and I drove down, and we were debating whether we should try actually to -- to -- to cross the bridge, but we were told by the soldiers on the Yugoslav side, the -- the Serb side of Yugoslavia, that they wouldn't -- we wouldn't be let across. So we decided just to park the car out of sight and Dragan was in the car and I sat on the hood with a radio listening to -- I think it was the BBC World Service and kind of looking down the bridge, trying to spot if anyone was coming across. And the first people that came across were two young women. And I said to Dragan, I said, Two people are coming. And I went and got in the car and Dragan got out and asked them if they needed a ride to where they were going and if they needed a ride, and they said, We're going to Ljubovija and yes, and it was still from -- you can see from the map here it was at least a kilometre or two away to the village itself, to the town itself. And I drove and Dragan started up conversation with them saying, Hey, you know, where are you from, and what are you doing? And one of them said that their -- their husband was in the Bosnian Serb forces and it was a mess over there, and we started to engage and ask them what was happening and then that's when they said, Well, what do you mean what's happening? How do you not know what's happening? Of course you know what's happening there. We insisted we didn't and that kind of surprised her. And then she began to talk about -- mentioned things that became very common to statements that we'd heard on the next days and on the next driving back and forth with other people, hangars and playgrounds and schools and -- mostly playing-field, playground, and hangar, and that men were being brought there and they were being killed, that most were being shot, that only the worst, the known war criminals, were having their throats cut, that it was obviously organised. In some cases there were people who were being -- there were calls that went out to people that if they wanted to take revenge on -- on men from Srebrenica that they were being held. And there was -- the interesting thing was -- or the most impactful thing was that these people were clearly not happy, none of them, and there was an element of shock, and they really were stunned that somehow this were a secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You mentioned before that you don't want to be either first or last with a story like this. What did you do once you heard this? How much corroboration did you feel that you needed before you could go to print with a story like this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, we pulled off the side of the road. I think it was the first time, I mean after the girls had gotten out, and we were slumped in the seats and Dragan was sitting in the passenger seat next to me, and I remember we just stared at each other for a long time and I think the thing I said was, Holy shit. And we looked at each other and we were -- you know, we were talking about 4.000. Are you sure? That's 4.000. And we said we had to go back and talk to more people, which we did, and then when we said that we'd obviously heard enough, that there was a constant -- the story seemed to be constant, we said we can't go to print with this. We have to figure out if this is an exaggeration or what's going on. We have to go back to Belgrade. So we turned around and we went back to Belgrade, and the idea was we wanted to know if other embassies were -- I mean, the Dutch Embassy had soldiers there. What were they hearing? What were the UN agencies hearing? Did the ICRC have anybody in? What about Serbian groups? Did they have any information about this? So that's what we figured we had to do. Then when we went back to Belgrade, because it was clear that Dragan Cicic and myself could not go over, we started contacting friends whom Dragan and I had worked with previously who we trusted -- whom we trusted and whom we had a relationship with, including Dragan's father Nikola, and we asked them if they would go over and have a look and take recorders or -- and take notes somehow on what they heard, and we told them what to ask in certain circumstances. And at the same time, we were told of other people who lived in that valley who either had relatives in Bratunac or were from Bratunac or had recently come back from Bratunac, so we decided that we would go back to the area and try to find more people from the region to see, you know, what they were hearing and what -- if -- what they might have seen, and that began a process at that lasted for another week. The first few days to corroborate the numbers, that large numbers of men were being killed, and then that eventually led to stories of killings further away from Bratunac-Srebrenica, along the Drina valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: When you finally went to print with this story for the first time on the 21st of July, at that point did you still feel like you were taking a risk with this story, or were you -- your information was solid by that point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I felt it was -- you know, it was very hard without having direct eyes yourself on the site, and even then, direct eyes, you would only see a portion of this. I mean -- but what was clear to me was that there were various execution sites in various places where large numbers of men were being killed. And it was clear from what people were telling us that the numbers were in the thousands, that it was not a small number of men. I was confident of that. However, I was still the only one out there with this information. None of my colleagues, for reasons I can't explain or not that I'm aware of, did they follow up and try to replicate what we did down in Ljubovija. I think maybe "The Times of London" did, which I think I found out about much later. But by and large, I was still the only one out there with the information and I was being denounced all over the place by pro-Serb groups as being a dupe and a lackey and obviously anti-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter number 3214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender this marked map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I would, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, if you can initial and date this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4405, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. 4405.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just for the record, this 3214 wasn't notified on our list but it's a better quality version of map 24 in our map book, which was notified on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could just focus on -- yeah, that part of the map. Mr. Block, ignore all those markings on the left-hand side of the map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Could you bring the map down a little bit, a little past Banja Koviljaca. Okay. There we go. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about in your statement in the days after first hearing this information in Ljubovija, you go to the area of Banja Koviljaca and start talking to people who hear or who have seen killings over the river. Can you mark for us the specific area where you went with these people.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It's on -- it should be okay. Well, first we went to Loznica here, and we started talking to -- to -- to people who said that they would go down, they would often fish or hang by the river, and they started to see bodies floating down the river, which was the talk of the town, and that some of them said that they had been hiking and that people in Banja Koviljaca had actually seen people shot and that there was -- someone who was shot was brought to the hospital. So we went to Banja Koviljaca. If you could bring the map up somehow. Can I do it with my finger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we need to mark the -- do the marking again. We'll do that again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. That's good enough. That's a little bit -- higher. So, Loznica is where we went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before marking you need to push the button, but please wait to be assisted by our usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. We first went to Loznica and then we went to Banja Koviljaca and we went with a group of people who had been out hiking that day, an elderly man and a couple, and they brought us -- as you can see from the map, it's topographical, that there are hills on this side. They brought us somewhere around here, just, you know, a little bit outside of Banja Koviljaca, and, you know, we asked them what they had seen. And they said that they saw people being pushed off of trucks and -- and people killed, and we said, well, where did you see it, and they were able to point directly across the river to -- to what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. For the record, you've put an X on the place where you went with these people.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: More or less, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you put an A on the spot where they were pointing to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, they were pointing across the river into this area more or less. That they were -- that they saw. It was very dramatic because it was -- it was definite. They knew exactly where they were pointing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, around this time, you also heard the story of the wounded Muslim lawyer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Right, we had heard that -- we had gone back to Banja Koviljaca and we had heard from people who said that there were stories of -- now, we'd originally heard this, that someone had been wounded and -- and we started to ask about, and they said, you know, Yes. Yes. Someone was in the river. He was crying out for help and people went in to take them. And we said, well, where did they take them, and he said to the sanitorium. So we turned around and went to the sanitorium and they showed us the -- the register of -- that they had been here but that the man was not there. His wounds were too severe and he had to go to the hospital in Loznica. So we decided to then go to Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And I know you've talked about this in your statement, but if you can briefly tell us again about what happened when you got to Loznica and spoke to the people at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It was clear that we were the last people on the planet that they wanted to see. They were not happy we were there. They were not happy we were asking questions. At first they denied that anyone had been brought there, but we grabbed the register and we saw that someone indeed was there and that there was a doctor's name. And we asked to see the doctor, and there was some consternation on their part that they couldn't find him, and, finally, they put some doctors together, and we sat down and we asked them about what had happened, and they said nothing had happened. And we challenged them with what we had -- with what we knew from the registries, what we heard from people who had actually put the man in their car and -- and all of a sudden their memory's, Oh, yes, yes, that man, yes, yes. I believe he was a lawyer, yes. But it wasn't very serious wounds, just scratches and surface injuries, but we really can't speak because we didn't treat him. The man who actually sewed him up is not here, but yes, I have a vague recollection, as they were twisting in their seats. And then, of course, they then said that after he was patched up that he was sent to Bijeljina and under guard was handed back to the Bosnian Serb authorities. And that's where the trail ended and that was where the story ended. The only other thing that I recall was that while on one hand the doctors at the Loznica hospital were very quick to dismiss their knowledge or any significance to this, they did seem to also justify that whatever happened to him, he -- he deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I get you to initial and date this map.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Block. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Block, as you noticed, your evidence-in-chief was admitted in writing mostly, in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Block. This is not a mere test. First of all, I'd like to thank you for being so kind as to meet the Defence, in other words, with me and Mr. Robinson. I hope it will assist us in dealing with this testimony expeditiously and efficiently. Tell us this, please: You said that you heard some things from a driver. You either don't know his name or do not wish to disclose it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: That's correct. I've not talked to him, so I don't want to put his name out there without at least his knowledge, but I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you who he had heard that from about me being upset?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I don't recall asking him. He was in Pale. Pale's a small town. When he told me that he'd heard that you were upset and that the general -- the Serb authorities were, you know, unpleased, I assumed that this was just common knowledge in -- in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you believe that everyone at Pale could know what I thought or could hear me speak. If I didn't say that in a public address, then it must have been said somewhere in the street, in your interpretation. How did people know how -- what I thought? Did you do any research on how he was familiar with this alleged position of mine?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: No -- no, I did not. As I said previously, the -- who -- who may have ordered the confiscation of the video at the time was not a prime concern of mine, and, you know, it's not uncommon, you know, in Pale, as well as in Belgrade, that, you know, many people were privy to conversations that people had in private. So I didn't think too much of it. I didn't give it -- I didn't think it was wrong. At the same time it was -- like I said, it was not something that I thought that I needed to focus on. It was just background information, and clearly, I think it was Zoran's intention to use the video to show the occupation and subjugation of Srebrenica in a positive light, and what was clear the footage did -- was actually much more damning, and I think that that was clear to anyone who saw it. So it was not out of the realm of possibility that someone would see this in the Serbian authorities of Bosnian -- Republika Srpska authorities and be upset that this had managed to make the airwaves and get international attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that due to my position, I was the object of journalistic attention and I could not even leave my office or express my opinion publicly without being taken note of by journalists?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, but you were not always, at this -- at this moment from, what I recall, you were not necessarily easy to reach. You know, there were lots of people that were -- you had to -- you know, a journalist, a foreign journalist, would have to go through to get to you, but, yes, you were -- you were obviously on the hot seat in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, and this thesis is somewhat corroborated by -- but let me go first back to what you said today and in our interview. Apparently for you it wasn't of great importance to establish whether it was indeed true that I reacted in that way. It seems that it wasn't as important to you then as it has now proven itself to be.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: It was just something that -- that I had heard. What was clear was that the video-tape was no longer there. What was clear was that there were instructions obviously from someone higher in the chain of command to bother to get this from Belgrade as well as, I understand, similar tapes from Republika Srpska TV. That was sufficient for me to understand that the tape was no longer freely available, and that's all that -- that mattered. Exactly who gave the order at the time was not important, and I think its importance now is only, you know, because of the current circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this remark or objection have to do with the fact which TV station edited and broadcast that? Was that a remark at the expense of Studio B, and did you know that they were our political opponent at the time as they are nowadays?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your -- your question about the objection, but what is clear is, yes, I mean, Studio B was something of a chameleon. It was not pro-Milosevic. It was pro-Serb. It was a little surprising to me that -- I was told that when the documentary aired that it had aired on Studio B, but one was always prepared for surprises in the former Yugoslavia. And again, I think that the intention of Zoran Petrovic in putting together the documentary was to portray something positive about the recapture of Srebrenica and I -- I don't think that his intentions or the intentions of Studio B were any other than this. I don't think they actually realised what they had, and I was -- from what I understood, the documentary was cut and put together very quickly. So again, the impression was that I think that they put together something that they thought was -- while was not propaganda was pro-Serb and didn't realise the potential damage that it -- it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was trying to see whether you heard someone remarking about a reporter being let inside Srebrenica with the approval of the RS authorities, and then his footage was shown on TV and broadcast by a TV station which was not our ally. Actually, it has always been our opponent. Was this element contained in the general remarks you could hear at the time about the airing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Nothing that I recall to this -- you know, to this effect. I do remember Dragan and I basically going, This was shown on Studio B? And we found it a bit strange, but beyond that, when we went in to see the footage, we were -- it was a Sunday. It was the -- the station was not very well staffed. They just gave us the tapes and we were able to look at them ourselves, and when we had trouble with equipment, they helped us out. I mean, no one said anything to the effect to basically give me the impression that the intention in airing this -- this documentary was meant to be damaging. And also the other thing to remember here is journalists had relationships with various editors and producers, and it was just my guess that whoever the producer was of this show had some relationship with Petrovic and that's why Petrovic was able to sell the -- the footage to him. I'm sure if he had a relationship somewhere else or with another station that had a kind of documentary slot, he would have sent it there. So I -- you know, initially, like I said, it was surprising, but I didn't -- I didn't -- I didn't think too much about it. Like I said, Serbian B [sic] was not pro-Republika Srpska, but it was very pro the larger Serbian cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think they would agree with that, but in any case, you corroborated that by an alleged statement given to you by Mr. Pirocanac. Did he tell you that there were objections to his presence there or that there were objections to Studio B airing it to their own benefit or for their own end?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: All I remember from that time period was that Zoran was very agitated. He clearly was under pressure. I think that the pressure -- it was my impression that the pressure had caught him off guard, the criticism had caught him off guard, and as we discussed, I think that he was in a very frustrating position because he had scored this tremendous journalistic coup of having access to this area, having footage that was very valuable, and at the same time was being seen as something of a traitor, and I think this is what was on his mind at the time. He was very upset that we had access to the footage, that we had used it without -- without his permission, that we didn't discuss it with him, and that -- and that his patrons in the -- in the Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb military were very angry with him, and that was the -- the main focus, that you don't realise how much trouble I had put him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who were these people supporting him? It's the first time that I hear of some patrons or bosses of his. I thought he was completely independent, and I still do. In other words, who could pressure him? Who was his employer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: A journalist is subject not only to pressures of their employer but also to sources and the people whose assurances they give. Sometimes someone will give you access to something in exchange for, you know, Don't get me into trouble over this. And you go, No, no, no, I would never get you into trouble. And I think that's -- I think he was in trouble from the people who trusted him and helped him get access to the area. I don't think it was bosses that he was in trouble from. In some ways, journalists can always deal with problems from their bosses. Sources on whom we depend sometimes are much more important for us to try to keep happy or at least to keep them on our good side, because this is how we were able to do business, by gaining people's trust and confidence. And if we're good at our job, we -- we -- we -- we are able to protect them and use the information or access that they gave us without ever implicating them or getting them in trouble, and I think he had -- he had managed to cross that line, and I think that's where he was feeling the pressure from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see this. Is it possible that he wasn't allowed to use the footage he authored? Was it understanding or understandable to you that he was upset with you working on that material without the approval of the author himself or was that unusual too?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: He certainly -- he certainly felt that that was what had been -- happened, what had been done, but the documentary surely was at this time inside the public realm. So whether I had access to this from Studio B or whether I had seen it on television that night, there's nothing that could be done to -- to -- you know, his arguments that I had no right to see this were ludicrous. The fact that Studio B had given us the rushes or some raw footage to view as well, that argument was between him and Studio B, not with me. And the final point was and I think we argued was that I didn't need his commentary because the camera to some degree spoke for itself, and, you know, what -- I didn't see why he -- I needed his permission to see something that had already aired, but he felt otherwise. He felt that this was his intellectual property and we had no right to access to it, and again, it was my impression that he was venting at Dragan and me because my story had gotten him in trouble because, you know, what was clear to me when viewing the footage is that it put the Bosnian Serb authorities in -- in a very tight spot because it showed men who were clearly visible and, therefore, in theory identifiable, in -- in Bosnian Serb authority hands alive, and therefore if they turned out to not be alive later, someone would have to explain what happened. So I thought that it was very naive of him to believe that -- that that footage was not explosive, but he did not see it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, shall we take a break? Half an hour. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to be heard very briefly on a procedural matter concerning the Court's indication that it would be ruling on Mr. Robinson's request concerning the Obradovic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be quick on this. I just wanted to remind the Court that Mr. Robinson sent two e-mails indicating that he would -- he intended to make a request concerning those matters. The Court issued its ruling on the first matter with respect to Mr. Lesic without being heard by the Prosecution. We're not revisiting that or disputing the Court's decision in that regard. However, before the Court makes a decision on this matter, we would like to be heard on Mr. Robinson's request. And as a general matter in future, we would anticipate that when Mr. Robinson signals his intention to make an oral motion in court, that he would be obliged to do so before ruling so that the Prosecution could respond. Thank you, Mr. President. And Ms. Edgerton, who will be calling Mr. Obradovic, will be here at the commencement of the next session if the Court wishes to hear argument on this issue from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we not hear from you? Everything is so fuzzy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is okay, can we hear from you now, Ms. Edgerton. We can hear it in the presence of Mr. Block. I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would be, of course, happy to do that, Your Honours, but given the time, and this would take a few minutes, I wouldn't want to postpone the break or interfere with the schedule of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not encroaching on the break time. If it is not that lengthy, I think I would like you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: How long do you think, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it would probably take me somewhere between seven and ten minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will then hear from you after the break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll begin, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just jump in briefly with getting back to you on the notification for Mr. Block. Having read the restrictions on that document, it shouldn't be publicly quoted, used in public session, or disclosed to other institutions, but simply referring to its title in the notification should be okay. So I think that can remain public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, just so we don't get this process inverted, Mr. Robinson mentioned to me that he wanted to actually put his request on the record before Ms. Edgerton argued. I don't know if he still has that in mind, but I didn't want to pre-empt that if that remained his intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I appreciate very much the Chamber being so efficient on my request and it's always my intention to notify the Chamber of issues that we intend to raise in advance so that it doesn't take you by surprise and doesn't ambush the Prosecution. But we -- if it doesn't -- if you don't mind, I'll just take a minute to put on the record our reasons for objecting to the 92 ter package for Mr. Obradovic. First of all, we think that the Prosecution, when they're benefiting from Rule 92 ter, ought to at the minimum make it as easy as possible for the other parties, including the Chamber and the Defence, and we'll do the same when it's our turn. And we think that dumping a 290-page transcript on us, which took me almost four hours to read, and containing many, many things that are not really targeted towards this case, such as the Main Staff's chain of command and hierarchy and things that were relevant to Mr. Tolimir, as well as the -- and information about Zepa and the prejudicial information about the proposed use of chemical weapons by General Tolimir there. So we believe that the Prosecution should have put together a statement of this witness that's more targeted to the Karadzic case, and because so much of the material, which I consider even more than half of it, is extraneous and in some ways prejudicial, we believe that the witness's testimony should be led live. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and I apologise for you having to turn your heads should you wish to look in my direction. To respond to Mr. Robinson's e-mail and his request today, I see there's two main areas I want to just talk about, the first being the size of the proposed 92 ter package of the witness, which is -- Mr. Robinson described in his original e-mail as burdensome. That's three days of testimony in the Tolimir case, which not only do I think is quite manageable for a witness of this nature, but should never be the only reason, Your Honours, for determining the admission of a 92 ter statement. The size of the package in and of itself isn't necessarily an obstacle for its admission, but actually the -- the assertions by Mr. Robinson that there's a large number of irrelevant topics in this witness's Tolimir evidence is something that we very much take issue with, and I was actually surprised to read this initially last week. Frankly, I think it's almost absurd to suggest that the inner workings of the VRS Main Staff are irrelevant to this case. They're integral. Dr. Karadzic was the supreme commander of the Bosnian Serb Army. The army was subordinated to him in law and in practice. The Bosnian Serb Army is alleged to have implemented the policies and goals of Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. The evidence of the structure, the effective function, the operation, the command principles, the drafting processes, the reporting and communications of this army offered by this witness, I would submit goes to the crux of the case against Dr. Karadzic. And just to make the point abundantly clear, I could refer Your Honours to our pre-trial brief on this, paragraphs 70, 119, and 125. And to just pull one example from there by way of synopsis, the Prosecution asserted that Dr. Karadzic and the Main Staff and civilian leadership were provided with accurate and timely information about events on the ground and asserted that reports from the corps level to the Main Staff were made orally and in writing and special reports which included information on enemy forces, the state of combat readiness of units of the corps, the situation on the ground and so forth. And just with that one example we can see that the evidence of General Obradovic underpins any number of these assertions and is directly relevant to these proceedings. And calling the events in Zepa irrelevant is, I'd submit, just another version of an argument Mr. Robinson's previously made in both oral and written submissions, and Your Honours have previously ruled on, and those with respect to events in Gorazde and Cerska, which are other areas of the eastern enclave. Dr. Karadzic isn't charged with events in Zepa in 1995. Nevertheless, those -- the evidence about those events as referred to and discussed during this witness's testimony in the Tolimir case is relevant for a number of reasons. It's clearly relevant to the overarching joint criminal enterprise to remove non-Serbs from Bosnian Serb-claimed territory from 1991 to 1995. It's relevant as pattern evidence. So even though outside the indictment per se, evidence of the policies of the Bosnian Serb leadership of blockade, convoy restrictions and attack against the Zepa enclave is relevant because the same pattern was supplied to Srebrenica and other locations in the enclaves. That pattern is evidence of the continued military operations to implement the third strategic objective. The evidence in Zepa are relevant as evidence that goes to Dr. Karadzic's command over the Bosnian Serb Army. It's relevant to support the assertion that the Bosnian Serb Army acted under Dr. Karadzic's direction. It's relevant to show effective communications and reporting within the Bosnian Serb Army, and it's actually also relevant, Your Honours, as evidence which goes to the crimes committed in Srebrenica in 1995. It confirms and corroborates the evidence of David Harland in his statement at P820, paragraphs 225 to 228, and there he discusses his involvement in complex prisoner exchange negotiations that lasted over ten days in the period of time surrounding the fall of Zepa. He talks about the Serbs initially insisting on a surrender but later pushing on an all-for-all prisoner exchange and notes with hindsight that it would appear, and I quote: "It would appear that this was because Mladic realised that once the Bosnians knew what had happened in Srebrenica, he had no chance of getting his prisoners back." The evidence related to Zepa corroborates, as I said, and confirms exactly what Mr. Harland describes, Serbs forces pushing to move quickly for an all-for-all exchange because once the full story of Srebrenica broke or came to light, they would have no chance of getting prisoners back. And we see this happening in the evidence and documents discussed by this witness in the Tolimir case. So if you consider evidence like this out of context, as Mr. Robinson would you have do, saying Zepa is irrelevant, its significance to this case is lost. It is clearly relevant. And just finally on what Mr. Robinson described as the proposed use of chemical weapons. Just one remark. After examination and cross-examination on this subject, it's quite obvious that the parties in the Tolimir case understood the document from which this initial point relating to chemical weapons arose meant to refer to chemical means or assets, in particular tear gas grenades. And the evidence in the proposed 92 ter package on this point shows -- is relevant because it shows that those assets were in the array of the Bosnian Serb Army, that they were delivered to the Drina Corps and the 65th Protection Regiment, and it goes then to corroborate the evidence -- the recent evidence of Mr. Nikolic who confirmed that members of this regiment were at Potocari -- pardon me, that they were attached to the VRS Main Staff and they were at Potocari separating people. And also this evidence goes to confirm the evidence that's come before this Chamber from KDZ045, a witness who was a survivor of the killings at Srebrenica who said that grenades with a poisonous gas were thrown by Bosnian Serb forces at Muslim men who had broken off from the column escaping towards Tuzla. So that covers all the points relating to relevance I wanted to address Your Honours on, and end with the submission that I think this witness's evidence is perfectly admissible under or pursuant to Rule 92 ter and clearly directly relevant and should be considered in context. And I don't think I have anything else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could just briefly reply. I think the argument that Ms. Edgerton made shows that this issue has taken on a larger significance than simply admitting something under 92 ter live because it now deals with how far you want to open the whole story of Zepa. General Tolimir was tried for Zepa events. It's in his indictment, and so the testimony that you -- from this witness was very broad and no objection was made. I think that that's an even better reason why you have to be careful to hear the witness's testimony live so we can determine what aspects, if any, of the evidence relating to Zepa should be admitted in this trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton and Mr. Robinson. The Chamber will consider the submissions and give its ruling after the next break. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So now it's a bit clearer to me. Mr. Pirocanac was exposed to pressures not only because his report was carried but because of your interpretation of that report; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: That's what I assume, or -- or at least that the -- that something -- that it became damaging, damaging to his -- to the people who had given him access and damaging something -- to something that I think was important to him. I don't know. I mean, you know, it's hard for me to say, but I think to -- to a larger Serb cause, and I don't think that he was happy with having that put on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said today on page 36, line 14: "My story was what got him into trouble." Right? We can go back to that page, if you will. So it was published. The material was published. It was edited. And it was broadcast by a station that did not really like us, but all of that did not bring Mr. Pirocanac under pressure. He was subjected to pressure after you published your story, your interpretation of his report. Is that the essence of what you said on page 36?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you would not have allowed someone to analyse your notes on the basis of which a text of yours was written? You publish a text and that's it, but your notes should not be analysed in public because that is not something that you had agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, but I wouldn't go leaving my notes around for other people to -- to use them or to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he left that at Studio B TV, not for the purpose of using it as public material. It was part of his work, but it wasn't supposed to be made public; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I think that would be correct. It was not part of the documentary which aired, but it was not my concern. I went in to see Studio B and asked them and they gave me the tapes. And I said, What is this? And they said, Here. It was the raw footage and the documentary. So I wasn't going to look a gift horse in the mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By the way, now that we've mentioned notes, during the interview you said to us that at your home in America, you may have some notes from that period of time. Could we count on your kindness, if you manage to dig them up, to provide us with your journalistic notes from that time? We will observe any restriction on publishing names, for instance, if that is what you ask for.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I would be happy to go back and look for my notes, but I do not think that I would be prepared to hand them over for a variety of reasons, not least of which would be the -- the jeopardy that it would be able to put sources in. I also think that it's not -- it's not appropriate in the sense that -- for the same reason that you were suggesting with -- with Mr. Pirocanac, that notes are themselves appropriate. We make the decisions on what is important when we -- when we write the stories. The other thing is, I'm not sure you'd be able to read my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I wonder if I could intervene here and try to be just a little bit more specific with Mr. Block. And that is that we were wondering whether or not he would be willing to look through his notes of his meeting with Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac on the 18th of July, 1995, and if there are any notes that exist of that conversation, to make a photocopy of them and send them to the Trial Chamber so that we could determine whether or not there was any reference made during -- to Dr. Karadzic in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you answer the question, Mr. Block?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe that I'm prepared to go that far, and I'll explain why. There are many in the journalist community who are opposed to assisting a body like this in the belief that somehow this exposes them to great ever danger, that somehow by testifying in a trial of this nature that somehow whatever veneer, thin veneer of objectivity and partiality we have, that somehow it's stripped of that.
