And I don't share that assessment fully. I believe that we are here in some ways in service of our journalism and that what we publish is what we deem to be important in how we weigh the information. It goes through a complicated process that is often rooted in time and by experience, and I think that being able to here to -- come here to be able to help give context and background to my reporting is one thing, but to hand over raw notes I think crosses a line that I'm not prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, would it be possible to be heard on an issue that arises from this, whether it be now to excuse the witness or at later time, but I think this would affect the admissibility of that aspect of his testimony and I'd like to be heard on that at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll be heard later on, Mr. Robinson. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take notes when you spoke to ordinary people that you refer to -- or, rather, you refer to the content of your conversations with them in your texts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. I was trying to think when you just asked me if I took notes when I spoke to Pirocanac. I mean, to be quite honest, I'm not sure I did because I think it was a conversation. There were some cases in which notes would be taken immediately, when you would sit in front of someone and you'd be taking notes. At other times you would have a conversation and you would record the gist of those conversations or you would jot down what was said in your memory, which is also reasons sometimes why we'll have recorders or when you report with another journalist so that you both agree to -- that you understand what was said. It's a question of what makes people nervous or what would make people comfortable. If someone becomes very nervous that you're sitting there taking down every word that they're saying, then it becomes counter-productive to being able to figure out -- to obtain information or to figure out what had happened. In a country like the former Yugoslavia which had a Socialist past, often standing in front of someone with a notepad was counter-productive to people explaining what happened. It gave them -- it seemed that they were being interviewed in a police-like situation. So yes, in some cases I had notes when I was sitting down directly in front of -- talking to people. And other times, the notes were constructed after they had -- after they had, for example, left -- left you or -- so I'm not sure again I understand the question, but, yes, when I talked to ordinary people I would take notes. Other times I just formed part of a general background that I was already aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll try to put questions to you that you'll find easy to answer by saying yes or no. I'm afraid we won't have time to cover everything in the time that has been allocated to me. Do you agree that in July 1995, we did not have a relationship with Serbia and President Milosevic? There was a quarrel between us, and the embargo on the border was still in force?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Not something that I can completely answer with a yes or no question [sic]. Yes, the official relations were strained, but there was still a tremendous amount of support that took place and a lot of -- there was a lot of smuggling that the authorities turned a blind eye to, and there was also a large amount of evidence to suggest that despite fact that Mr. Milosevic was not fond of you, that when it came to providing support to make sure that the Republika Srpska project did not collapse, he would swallow his pride and make sure you had what you needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I was going to object to the vagueness of the question, just the reference to a relationship, but I think the witness handled it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this much you knew about our conditions. You agree that Serbia requested that we accept the Contact Group plan and only humanitarian items went through, and the political leadership had no contact. The political leadership of the two sides had no contact at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Again, yes, it is true that Milosevic supported the Contact Group plan on the surface, but I do think that both sides had various ways to pass messages when the time came. An example of this was that I would often be able to be in Belgrade and know exactly what was happening in Pale and in other areas of Republika Srpska, and I heard this information often through political channels close to President Milosevic, and the information that I would receive would -- would -- would be validated. So when -- yes, I do not think that you were -- it is my impression that the -- while you may not have been talking, that you were able to exchange messages when you needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you exclude the work of the secret services? Do you accept that the Serbian Secret Service was operational in Republika Srpska without me being aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 18, line 20, today you said that you not only heard that the Serbian leadership was very angry, you also heard that the government of the Bosnian Serbs had confiscated this tape. Do you believe that under such conditions in which we had a quarrel with official Belgrade, do you believe that under such conditions we could have confiscated some tape from some television channel that wasn't favourably disposed towards us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second before you answer. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that's starting to get -- call for a very speculative answer from the witness. What means were available to the RS government to get a tape cannot be something within this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If he knows -- can he not answer as far as he knows? Yes, please proceed, Mr. Block.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I can say is that Republika Srpska clearly had government organs in Belgrade, including a press office and places where, you know, the officials of the intelligence services would have access to each other. I don't think it was beyond the purview or reach of the Republika Srpska to make a request and be allowed to confiscate the tapes. At the same time, I'm under no illusion that the tapes did no favour to the Belgrade government of Mr. Milosevic. So I think it was in everyone's interest to make these tapes go away. And again, if what Dr. Karadzic is asking me is if the tapes could have been confiscated from a Belgrade TV station without Mr. Milosevic's permission or without the Yugoslav intelligence community's permission, I think he's right. There would have been very little chance of that. But I think in this particular case you would not have any argument between the two that these were best to -- to disappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure this is a translation issue. In your question you said Mr. Block said, page 18, line 20, the government of Bosnian Serbs had confiscated this tape, but I don't think this is what Mr. Block said. He said Bosnian Serb authorities confiscated, and then it was military leadership, to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps I misspoke, but the authorities, not the government but the authorities of the government in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Block, I don't dispute the fact that you heard something. I bring into question the source that said it was possible for this to happen in the middle of Belgrade in Studio B that wasn't favourable to us and they would publish that. If Milosevic had intervened at all, they would have broadcast everything. They would have made it known. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: As I said previously, Studio B was a bit of a chameleon. They were critical when they wanted to be critical and were cheerleaders when they wanted to be cheerleaders. Trying to guess what area, what mood they were in at the time was not very important to me. We were told by Studio B that there were Bosnian Serb authorities that came by to collect the tape, and I had no doubt that -- that they knew the difference between Yugoslav authorities and people who were coming in from -- representing an outside authority, and I took them at their word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Pirocanac was there with the approval of the authorities and a high-ranking police official?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's, I believe, what -- what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, and I informed you about this in the course of the interview, I asked whether you could check, that I agreed that Peter Arnett, a well-known journalist, should follow the events in Zepa and that he should be able film them with a camera. And this is what he, in fact, did.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I checked and that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did Pirocanac himself tell you in relation to me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I just recall that he said that he understood or that he had heard that you were -- you were angry at the broadcast of his documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Prosecution published an interview with Mr. Pirocanac and went through those tapes second by second, so to speak, in the year 2006?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I -- I know that they had -- that investigators had talked to Mr. Pirocanac about -- about some missing sections in the tape. I don't have any insight into what exactly they discussed or what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you find out that the investigator here testified that perhaps 20 seconds were missing that were accidentally deleted in the course of the conversation and Pirocanac commented on the whole tape with them? And we have this here. We have the material that was broadcast on -- by Studio B here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I just want a cite for the investigator who testified that 20 seconds were missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blaszczyk testified and said that he saw the button being accidentally pressed that deleted 20 seconds at the most and he testified to this effect recently. Mr. Blaszczyk is the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, are you satisfied with this clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I would like a specific cite, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are contending the amount of time that was deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That would be the starting point. I don't think Mr. Blaszczyk could have seen the deletion of the footage that is at issue here. So I want to look at what section of the transcript he's citing to, to see exactly what Mr. Blaszczyk was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue in the meantime. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was as follows -- I'll move ahead and wait until we find the relevant page in the transcript, but my question -- the question I wanted to ask was as follows: I wanted to show what Mr. Pirocanac said in relation to myself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 65 ter 454761 [as interpreted], this interview between Mr. Blaszczyk and Nicholls with Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac, who obtained his Ph.D. in the meantime and is now involved in research, scientific research. It's the first page. Could we see page 112 in the English version, please. Perhaps we don't need the Serbian version, unless it's for the benefit of the public. From line 23. Could we have a look at the part that starts at line 23. This doesn't look like the same page that I have. Perhaps something isn't quite in order. Could we see the part where it says "Krajisnik." The page where it says "Krajisnik." I see. We need to move ahead three pages. That's the page we need. It's page 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look here and see what Mr. Pirocanac's answer is. Have a look at the part that starts at line 16, for example. And then line 20, it says: [As read] "The leadership of Bosnian Serbs, Krajisnik, and others asked [In English] Studio B and me to send them a copy the same as the next day it was aired, and I remember and I know the guy. His name is Zoran. He is now on "Politika." He could confirm that we sent by bus a copy to them, to Pale. They were still together. I don't know if Karadzic saw it, but most of them saw it. And if there they -- if you ask Krajisnik now if he remembers that, that it was very well done. This is -- my conclusion is that this was the moment they were -- and they heard about what's going on and they could stop to the completely --" and so on. [Interpretation] Briefly, Pirocanac had information according to which the Serbian side requested a copy and not the original. The copy was sent, and the Serbian leadership thought that this had been done very well, that the report he made was a good one.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: If that was the -- if that were the case, then I do not understand the reason for his agitated state when I saw him two days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see Mr. Nicholls [as interpreted] is up, but I'd like to have a look at the part that starts three pages later. Should I put my question to the witness or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Just -- yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to go back to this -- Dr. Karadzic's question on page 53, line 17, where he put to the witness that Mr. Blaszczyk testified and said that he saw the button being accidentally pressed and deleting 20 seconds at the most, and he testified to this recently. And I think what Mr. Karadzic is referring to is at transcript page 23609. Mr. Blaszczyk was testifying specifically about the Kravica warehouse footage, about the length of that particular piece, and he didn't say anything about seeing the button pressed and being accidentally deleted. So I'm not sure if it was a translation error or misunderstanding, but I think basically everything in that question was a misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see the part that starts three pages later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that part, Mr. Block, when material is provided, sold, or being bought, do colleagues get involved in bargaining of some kind or certain policies are pursued? Is the price increased and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. Someone in the broadcast world, when you have unique footage, then, yes, it is up for grabs, so to speak, and often available to the highest bidder. Sometimes a broadcast journalist can -- can sell initial access to a buyer with the understanding that he will then later release the footage to others at a less expensive price. So the various networks or TV stations will fight to have the right to the footage first. And it also varies from market to market. Sometimes, you know, you get the highest price for the first airing of it. In -- in, for example, the United States because it is a rich country and it has a large market you would ask one price, but you would demand a smaller price in a country like the Netherlands. But if they wanted to be the first one to broadcast some unique footage that you had, chances are you would ask them for a high price.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Mr. Pirocanac, if we bear all that in mind, increase the value of his work by saying how much it cost him and by referring to the pressure he was under? Can you find an explanation for this, because you can see what he says here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Okay. You're asking me a little bit -- I don't know because I'm not in the -- I was not in the broadcast world, although I do understand how it works. I had the impression in part that one of the reasons that he was irritated with me was because he felt that we had in a sense broadcast his tape, although it was done in writing, without any kind of compensation or permission, and that was part of the issue. When you talk about the missing sections, and I don't know if you asked me a question about that earlier, if I was aware of the missing sections, but I was aware of the missing section almost immediately, because very soon after the tape went missing, copies -- Zoran was -- was making deals with television stations for footage, and the footage that he was selling them did have these gaps in it, which seemed to be rather convenient because they happened to be over the -- the parts that were the ones that I had seen and reported on and seemed to be the most problematic for -- for -- for him or for his sources. I never saw the footage that I saw that original day in Belgrade until years later when I think a Dutch television station had managed to unearth a copy and asked me if this was what I had originally seen. So, yes, I believe, and this is also what I understand from friends that Zoran and I have in common, was that he was sitting on a journalistic gold mine of sorts. He had footage that everybody wanted. He also had footage that seemed to put him crossways with his sources and benefactors inside the Bosnian Serb and Yugoslav military establishment, so he had to find a way in which he felt that he was able to benefit journalistically and financially from what he had. And what I believe what the result was, was the footage that has become familiar to many of us now, which is the tape with gaps in it, and I think that in this way he felt that -- obviously he sold these pieces so he knew that -- what he was doing, and I can only speculate as to why the gaps and how those gaps occurred, but I think that in his mind, that without those sections, it was less problematic for him with his -- with his sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look at the previous page. The pages are a little muddled because of the printing. Have a look at the part that starts at line 18. It says: [As read] "[In English] So I don't remember who, but they were, for sure, contacted and they sent a copy. And the -- the return of this was -- I was told by somebody that it was very well done, very honestly, journalistically and objectively. It's interesting now when you see all the people there and who was in what -- what this meant exactly, you know. So maybe it's useful for you to -- for you for somebody [sic] else." Probably to ask somebody else. [Interpretation] Did you know that I was still on good terms with Mr. Pirocanac, and afterwards, after that event, I gave him a lengthy interview, and that was also the case in the course of the war prior to that event?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I did not know this until you informed me about it the other afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you just mentioned the civilian authorities, but you also mentioned the military. Do you agree that we had our conversation in this building and not in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. We met here, not far away, last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why we met here and not in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I assume it's because you had finished the day's hearings and that it was just more convenient to meet here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't the case. It's because the Detention Unit administration won't allow journalists in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness mentioned the army. If the Detention Unit will not accept journalists, how would the army at the front line accept journalists? I wanted to ask him whether someone else like Pirocanac could have been present at the front line. The army has its position about such matters. The civilian authorities had a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that given that Pirocanac had police authorisation and Peter Arnett had my authorisation, the civilian authorities didn't impose any restrictions under such conditions, but when we're dealing with the army, well, that's a different matter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I think what you're asking me is did I -- do I realise that the military put restrictions on journalists. Absolutely. And did civilian authorities -- were they able to overcome those -- those restrictions? Is that what you're asking me? Yes. The military did put restrictions on journalists, and often from my experience was if you had permission from civilian authorities, they did not always trump military orders in the field. And this would not necessarily come from even high up. You could have low-level officers or non-commissioned officers basically refusing to honour a piece of paper or a delegate who had been sent to accompany you. Often this was done, from my experience, because they were not informed, they did not hear the order directly from their superior, and they did not want to make a mistake. I -- to be quite honest, it was -- you could get in trouble for allowing a journalist entry to an area. You could never get in trouble for not allowing a journalist into an area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Block, now, you mentioned that -- the now-familiar footage with the gaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us what is the -- how long the period were of those gaps at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never timed them myself, but there was one in which I remember the commentary over them. They were -- there was one short gap in which I believe someone was playing with children or talking to children and you hear children's voices, and then in another section you heard Zoran apparently -- or someone talking about a shell on the ground, and that was of longer duration. All I remember was what seemed to me to be that was most glaringly excised from what was made available to journalists were the scenes in front of the warehouse at Kravica and scenes in front of the white house where they were pictures on -- of Serbian -- of Bosnian men from Srebrenica being detained. There were a lot of -- there was a lot of footage that I had seen that was from the raw footage that I've never seen duplicated anywhere, but clearly from that tape that I remember that he made available, those seemed to be the two missing sections. In terms of the length, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpreters, Your Excellency. Can we have a look at the transcript, page 23575, lines 9 through 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blaszczyk says: "[In English] Yes, that's correct. This footage is not -- not on the raw material handed over to us, and if we compare the time-code from the raw material, we see that originally there is missing about 11 seconds of recording." [Interpretation] So the whole gap lasts for only 11 seconds as established by the investigators. And that's the only difference between that and the raw material they received. Do you take the investigator's word for it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's with respect to specific footage. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That was going to be my observation, Mr. President. There's a number sections that are missing, and again this is a reference to a specific section, not a combination of the times of all of the missing sections. So Mr. Karadzic needs to be very clear when he's putting these times to Mr. Block what the significance is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the next page there is a reference to 24 seconds missing. That seems to be the time I noted. No, not the next page but page 23609. [As read] "[In English] Definitely it was the part these 24 seconds recorded over in the raw footage where we see the ratio package and the blank portion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is something that I am interested in a lot. Were you in a situation to verify what you could hear from your sources? Were you in a position to verify it, and did you invest an effort to check the accuracy of what you were told?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: In -- in reference to the numbers of people killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First and foremost concerning me being angry and that the Bosnian Serb authorities confiscated the tape. Well, to tell the truth, you did say today that it wasn't important to you, but were you otherwise in a situation to verify the accuracy of what you heard from someone else, which is second- or third-level hearsay, something you weren't able to observe yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Okay. In the case about the rumours of you, as I said, no, I never made any attempt to corroborate them. They were not a subject of -- of reporting. In terms of validating whether the tapes were confiscated under the orders of the Bosnian Serb authorities, yes, I validated that. And I find it very interesting to look at the section of Mr. Petrovic's statement when he talks about that copies were requested. Language was a very interesting issue in the former Yugoslavia, and one man's request is often another man's order for confiscation. So I don't think that there is necessarily a problem. What ends up happening is that tapes were sent to Pale, as I understood, at the request or orders, depending on how you want to term them, from the Bosnian Serb authorities and indeed that's where they went, and the tapes were never seen again as far as I am aware. And I did validate the fact that the orders came from the Bosnian Serb authorities. Again, when it came to the fact that I had heard that you were mad, no, I did not put any reporting energy into validating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the army, too, had a camera on site and that on that military footage we can see Pirocanac's camera? In other words, did you know that the army, too, were taping some of the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I had understood that there were -- not only that the army was taping it, that some units had their own video cameras, and that also that Republika Srpska TV had a journalist who had managed to make it to the Bratunac area and was also doing some filming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now focus on some other topics. You published an article, and I will ask for it to be shown in e-court. It was on the 14th of July. Can you tell us how an article is created and sent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: There's not a single answer to that. Effectively, articles can be ordered by editors, in some case even publishers. More often than not, however, if a reporter has a particular beat or area of expertise, he is expected to -- he or she are expected to cover that area as best they can and to provide a regular flow of stories and information. I was very familiar with the eastern area of Bosnia along the Drina River. Actually, I had -- was in Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, just before the Srebrenica attack had occurred. I had flown there and had been working on getting an interview with General Ratko Mladic, and once I had secured the interview and published it, I decided to go back home and see my family, only to find out a few days later that there was a military build-up, which actually I think it was just beginning as I left, in the eastern area. The attack commences a few days after I'm back, I believe, and at that time when Srebrenica fell, I was asked by my editors to see if I could call sources and the authorities and the press centres in Belgrade and in Pale and speak to humanitarian agencies through the numbers that I had that were in Zagreb and Tuzla, as well as in Belgrade, and try to get a little bit more information behind what was coming across on the wire agencies which most newspapers and radio stations and TV stations rely on when they don't have their own people in the area. And so I had read the reports that were coming across the agencies, the wires, as we call them, and then made a few phone calls into the area to say this is what Reuters is saying, or this is what the AP is saying, this is what "The New York Times" is carrying. Is this accurate? Is this so? What are you hearing? And, you know, like everything else, you weigh the information based on who is reliable to you in the past and how much detail they have, and a story is put together. Once a story is put together, it then needs to be able to fit in a space that it's allotted in the newspaper or even on air, and that often involves editing. Sometimes your editor will come back to you and demand that you have an allegation or assertion in a story that does not appear to be backed up by the information that follows, and you may be asked to go back and to get more information or a decision may be to cut it out. Often the worst fights that happen between editors and reporters is over how much space they're given to tell their story, and then what kind of cuts are made to the story. Usually on stories like this where I am not on site, I would be given much less space to tell a story than if I were actually there at the time. But that's -- that's a quick snapshot of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P4396. It was admitted today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Were you able to observe that the opposing sides were trying to smear each other and that they were one-sided? In other words, they were not objective concerning each other's activities. Were you able to see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Absolutely. If -- there seemed to be a -- a tendency, indeed an obsession in the former Yugoslavia for everyone to make a mad dash towards victimhood, and anything that ever happened was immediately announced and exaggerated, and often massacres would be inflated and atrocities would be exaggerated. This was very common, and it made our job harder because it sometimes could take months to untangle the stories. But it was -- you know, this was not a secret to any of us in the foreign press corps, to any of us covering the former Yugoslavia that -- that everyone was there trying to present their cause in the best light and to -- to, as I say, make a mad dash towards presenting themselves as the true victims. Victimhood seemed to be the justification that every side used to -- to inflict revenge and to kill the other side. So it seemed to me that everybody wanted to -- to have their victims and to display them in the most sometimes macabre fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that regard, do you agree with me that in the first paragraph you adopt from someone the term that they were deported, and in the next paragraph, apparently 40.000 people were trucked away. Were you able to get information about the meetings of General Mladic and Muslim representatives who were asking to leave, and did you have information that it was the UN who asked that the civilians in Srebrenica be allowed to leave, which was something that was going on around the time of this article. Actually, before it, because the meetings in question took place on the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: This was an initial report from the -- from the front lines. It was in response to agency reports and what had been coming out of -- from information that had been coming out from the UNHCR in Tuzla. The process behind it all was not at this time clear, I think, to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The article was probably written on the 13th if it was published on the 14th; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line [as interpreted] four -- well, you did put it in quotation marks, but apparently there were alarming news about two girls who were separated by the Bosnian Serb Army. Did you attempt to verify whether it indeed happened? It is in paragraph four of the text.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: No. I was just reporting what had been told to me by UNHCR officials from what they had heard. Again, these were very initial reports coming out, and at the time I believe I was in London, so it would have been very difficult for me to have done more than quick interviews. As I said in response to your question earlier, you will notice that this story is not very long and precisely it's because it wasn't any kind of enterprise journalism. It was a response to the events that we had heard, and it was our attempt to verify very quickly and just give a very quick overview of what information was coming out of the area. As a matter of fact, it was -- immediately after I wrote this story, I was sent home to pack my bags and to get ready to fly to Budapest where I would be picked up and given a ride into Belgrade. So I wrote this story, and I ran home and went to Yugoslavia to try to provide greater understanding and context to the initial stories that were coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So one needs to take into account that such initial texts had to be shorter and incomplete; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I don't know if I would say "incomplete," but you -- the scope of your information was much more limited by virtue of the fact that you were speaking on phone lines to -- which were sometimes very unreliable and you couldn't always get ahold of what you -- you know, who you wanted to, and so there's no substitute to being there or being as close as you can. And under the circumstances, I think this was the best and most complete job that we could have done at the time and recognising that is why I think my bosses and I agreed that I should immediately go back to -- to Belgrade and to try to get to the area to -- to figure out what was rumour and what was fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 21961. It may well be a P exhibit by now. P4398.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have the name of the person, the woman, you talked to concerning this information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: There were -- there are two, and, yes, we got their names at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the names, please, so that we can check the information they had then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: If I wanted their names known, I would have published them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you mentioned exaggerations. Were you able to confirm through later research the information contained in paragraph 3 about a field in Bratunac knee-deep in blood? Today it was page 11, line 20, in the transcript. Is this an exaggeration, or are you able to confirm that there were killings in that field knee-deep in blood? Were there any killings at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Let me go down a little further into the article, if I may, and see if I can find something that I think is very important. The next -- the next page, I believe, it's on. Is there a second page of the article? Okay. First off, if you read on the article, you'll also see very carefully that I question -- I give myself some leeway, because, you know, numbers are very difficult to validate in these kinds of circumstances. There was enough information to indicate that, as I said, large numbers, and I was reporting what I was told and I [indiscernible] say if the numbers are accurate. But what I want to do is in the next two paragraphs, we talk about how until now: "News of Bosnian Serb atrocities against Muslims who tried to flee the fallen 'safe areas' has been emerging from the testimony of refugees from Srebrenica for over a week, and the Bosnian authorities estimate 10.000 people are still unaccounted for. "But the horrors ... now surfacing come from Serbs, not Muslims, and refer specifically to men who surrendered or men who have been taken prisoner. It will be difficult for the Bosnian Serb authorities to dismiss their accounts as enemy propaganda." Now, the reason I put these paragraphs in there was precisely -- goes back to the very reason that Dragan and I were in the car and had this holy shit moment, when we turned to each other trying to digest what we had just been told about how the killings were taking place and the sheer numbers, and that is, usually the exaggerations and the overemphasis on killings was always done by each side. It seemed that Croats were always happy to talk about the number of Croats killed in a particular incident and to exaggerate the numbers, and Muslims did the same and Serbs did exactly the same. What was very unusual about this case were that these were not the victims talking about themselves. These were, in fact, the Serbs talking about the people that they were supposedly killing, about the number of people -- and this was extraordinary, because I had never come across that before. And this is why it was so shocking and this is why we ran back to Belgrade, because we figured if -- if this news had been crossing in to Serbia proper and it was as well known as these people claimed it was, then obviously this news had to be known by people with greater visibility into the area than I had, which is why we bent back. So the answer was, first off, that the exaggeration did not apply in this case to the same degree because it did not make sense that Bosnian Serbs would want to exaggerate why they were killing so many people. It didn't -- if any case, the usual practice were to basically downplay the number of people you killed to justify, you know -- to counter the enemy propaganda of how many people they claimed were killed. So that was the first thing. To answer your question, what we were able to validate was, as I said in my earlier testimony, was that the playground and the hangar were themes that had constantly come up in conversations with people who had been in that area, and the expression "krv do kolena," "blood to your knee," was something that I had heard for the first time, the expression, in this area and I had heard it repeatedly. So whether it was a figure of speech or not, it certainly was something that was in common currency and was an allegation that was surfacing continuously, again, from Serbs from Serbia who had access to the region either for family reasons or they wanted to see what was happening and from the Bosnian Serbs themselves who either had fled the area or had gone back to the area because they fled the area earlier and wanted to see what was happening. So this was not something that I was told only once but actually had been told repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be very good if we had more time so that your answers could be that lengthy, but I have to ask you for answers that are as short as possible because of our lack of time. In the next paragraph you say: "[In English] The reasons suggested for the reported brutality go back to the first year of the war when Muslim soldiers from Srebrenica managed to break the siege of the town and razed several nearby Serb villages, killing many Serb civilians in the process. "Now that the Srebrenica enclave has been overrun, the Bosnian Serbs want revenge." [Interpretation] You wrote about Bjelovac [Realtime transcript read in error "Bijeljina"], the torching of Bjelovac. We'll take a look at that later. Do you agree that Serbs around Srebrenica were angry at Oric and the Serbs, say, around Trebinje were angry at someone else? Did you see for yourself that these animosities were the result of mutual killings, that they were localised and aimed against specific persons in specific areas? It's not Bijeljina, it was Bjelovac. The transcript -- for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian population around Srebrenica was extremely hostile to the inhabitants of Srebrenica and to their military, towards their military commanders, and in particular Naser Oric who commanded them. It was no secret, and I think that the anger and the hatred was perhaps more intense in this area precisely because Oric was particularly successful, perhaps more successful than any other area of -- of Bosnia, in fending off Bosnian Serb attacks and indeed being able to strike seemingly at will in attacking Serb villages in the area. So I think to most Serbs, particularly Bosnian Serbs from the region, but I think much -- in a much wider area, Srebrenica represented a red flag. It was an open sore that was rather infuriating to them. So I think, yes, there was a lot of prejudice and a lot of hatred on a local level on a lot of areas. It was just more so in the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you don't want to tell us the name of this woman, can you tell us whether she was a person in authority or was she an ordinary person, the woman who told you about the numbers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: She was the wife of a Bosnian Serb officer, or she described herself as the wife of a Bosnian Serb officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, you tell me when the time is right. For the break, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break, if it is convenient, for an hour. And we'll resume at 1.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, the Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the accused's request that Ljubomir Obradovic be heard live. The Chamber notes that in his 290-page transcript from the Tolimir case which is sought for admission under Rule 92 ter, the witness gives detailed evidence about the structure and functioning of the Main Staff. The Chamber considers that, contrary to the accused's argument, this evidence is relevant to the charges in the indictment. The Chamber further notes that the witness provides ample evidence about events in Zepa after July 1995, which are not charged in the indictment. The Chamber does not consider that the evidence with respect to Zepa is irrelevant in that it maybe useful to better understood the aftermath of the Srebrenica alleged events of July 1995 and the alleged overarching joint criminal enterprise. However, if the entire transcript in the Tolimir case is to be admitted, it may be difficult for the accused to understand how much the Prosecution is relying on the evidence relating to Zepa and how much he should cross-examine such evidence. In conclusion, the Chamber sees no reason to order that this witness be led live and therefore considers that the evidence of this witness may be received under Rule 92 ter, but orders that Prosecution redact from the transcript the evidence related to Zepa and present this evidence live to the extent it deems it necessary in the context of these proceedings. That given, let's continue. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now please take a look at this text by your colleague, 1D5113. You certainly know that Mr. Cicic wrote texts as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be zoomed in a bit for the witness. So this is his text or his article. He worked for AIM from Belgrade. Can we now scroll down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that paragraph where it says "UN representatives"? Mr. Cicic is speaking about celebrating victory and that not all shots are proper gunfire. There is "senluk" which is a Turkish word for celebratory gunfire. Did you see that for yourself, that there was quite a bit of shooting apart from battle, when something was being celebrated, that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. And I think in the text of my other article I had someone who'd send someone in who'd heard some shooting and was told the same thing, that this was celebratory gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this paragraph we also see a confirmation of what you said to us today, namely, that revenge played a very important role. And Mr. Cicic says that there were killings without execution squads and that people who had someone to avenge were actually called in. Some people accepted that and others did not. Is that your experience as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: That is -- that's what we heard. I believe I came to a slightly different conclusion than Dragan, though, that it was a little bit more methodical than how he portrays it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. It refers to the stadium down here as a location that was a possible defence centre. "[In English] A few journalists who did get permits to go to Pale after the Serbs had conquered Srebrenica were explicitly told that they could take the road via Visegrad only, and it is quite impossible to get to the region of Srebrenica and Bratunac by this road." [Interpretation] Was it also your experience that the fighting in the woods went on a lot longer and that roads were not safe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: We were told, and I think it was General Mladic who made a statement saying that there were people trying to break out of the area and that there was fighting and people being killed. It was not clear immediately to us where -- where the fighting was and how intense it was, but we were aware that -- that there was some fighting going on and that some men had been captured in -- in the activity of -- of -- of fighting, and they had either surrendered or been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at the last paragraph, please: "[In English] A Pale television crew managed to make a shot of the prisoners at the stadium, but the film was confiscated by military authorities. No violence against the confined men could be seen on the film." [Interpretation] Is that what you also heard or learned, that the Serb television from Republika Srpska had their film taken away from them by our army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard the same, and I believe that what Dragan is referring to is the same footage that we saw on a -- on the football field at the stadium where prisoners were being made to stand up and sit down and stand up and sit down. So there was no violence, but the men were on the field, and they were clearly being ordered to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page of this text. The last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this text? Do you believe me if I say that there is no mention of my asking for something to be kept from the media -- or, actually, should I let you read the whole text?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Which is the last paragraph you're referring to, "The destiny of wounded Muslim soldiers?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] The leadership from Pale agreed to enable their evacuation to the hospital in Tuzla by mediation of the International Red Cross." [Interpretation] It's a reference to the wounded but I'm asking you about the entire text. Would you like to read all it or are you going to trust me that, apart from this confiscation that was carried out by the army vis-a-vis our own television, he does not mention at all any kind of interference on my part. Do you trust me on that or would you like to read all of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: No, I've read the text after you presented me with it last week, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, this text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2084, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5116 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D5516"]. Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My legal advisor Mr. Robinson e-mailed Mr. Cicic and now I'd like to show you this. The letter of Mr. Robinson is at the bottom of the page, as usual, and on the top of the page you see Mr. Cicic's answer. Mr. Robinson is asking about the meeting with Pirocanac, and he's asking whether he spoke about any anger on my part and so on. The questions are less important, but here are the answers: "[In English] Dear Mr. Robinson, in response to your query, I do remember that Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac said that he got in trouble with the authorities of Republika Srpska because of his footage. I do not recall whether he specifically mentioned Dr. Karadzic by name, though I did assume at that time that his reference included all the people in the leadership of Republika Srpska. "I hope this is answer to [sic] your question. "Sincerely, Dragan Cicic." [Interpretation] So do you agree that as far as Mr. Cicic is concerned that it was not noteworthy, otherwise he would have remembered that? Don't you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: As I said in my earlier responses to some of these questions, I don't think it was really at the time in any way relevant. It was clear that the authorities of Republika Srpska had ordered it. We had some validation of this information, and I left it at that. I remember Pirocanac saying that you were mad; Dragan doesn't. But again, it's not something that we went out to devalidate. It wasn't something that was of any particular significance at that time other than the fact that the authorities had said, you know, We need that tape. That tape was surrendered and it was not seen again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 22, 1D05116. That would be the right number. Thank you. Now I'd like to show your article from 1994. Let us please -- actually, can this document be admitted, I mean the e-mail, the correspondence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's necessary given that you read out all the -- all the text. Let's follow our practice. We will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 1D05117. Could we have that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this text about arms smuggling into Bosnia at the time, and is this text correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes. I think that history has shown this text is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the bottom of the page as well, although I'm sure that you're familiar with the entire text. All right. And now could we have the next page, please. "[In English] This strongly contrasted with the US reaction in September 1992, when a similar Iranian plane landed in Zagreb loaded with machine-guns, munitions and military personnel. Then the Americans not only blew the whistle on the plane but forced a reluctant Croatian government, which at that time was allied to the Bosnian Muslims, to intercept the plane and turn it back." [Interpretation] So as the war went on, more and more leeway was given to the Muslims to bring in more and more weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, and as well as fighters from outside the area came in as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2085, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D05118, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Even before that text you were aware of the background of the war and of the arming; right? Do you remember this text that you co-authored with Leonard Doyle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, Leonard was "The Independent's" UN correspondent at the time in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the text please be displayed for the witness to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us when you'd like to see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Has time confirmed this knowledge concerning the Albanian mafia that is now playing the lead role in the smuggling of heroin in Europe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: At the time, my understanding was that it seemed clear that that was the case. What I don't know is -- I mean, this was -- I think our evidence was being based on what police inspectors were suspecting. I wondered many years later when the Kosovo conflict broke open with Yugoslavia whether the arms were being stockpiled for their own use, but that was just my own question. But there is no doubt about it that the Albanian mafia was very involved in heroin, weapons, and cigarette smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bosnia, as we can see in the first paragraph, was also involved in these illegal armings; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Without a shadow of a doubt, the Bosnians were -- were looking for sources of weapons for wherever they could get it, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D05112. Could we have that called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this text? It's 1995, just before the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll down a bit. Was there a bit of excessive enthusiasm in this text? Do you think that you overdid it a bit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Overdid it in what sense, that I focused too much on General Mladic or that the reaction of the crowd was overstated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I mean the psychiatric diagnosis. You're not a psychiatrist yourself, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, we don't write headlines. We're just humble reporters. The editors have the privilege of excess in headlines. But, no, I'm not a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? Can we have a look at page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is where you mention me as well. In the context of disagreements with the military. Do you remember these elements from this page?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D2087.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the amalgamated statement, you mentioned that Sonja, my daughter who was in charge of the press centre, mentioned that you'd be in danger if you were to come to Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Well, that we would be arrested was the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the interview, you confirmed that you knew that she is not the one who arrests people, and you confirmed that you understood that when applying for accreditation at the press centre, she had to ask the security services, the State Security Service, and the military security service; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Correct, but I also took from her statement that she was certainly not going to argue our case, and she had no desire to see us there either. Dragan and I were not very popular, especially after the -- the story about the Petrocanac [sic] video, and I think even before that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D05111. Can we have a look at that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I think that this was a friendly warning, and perhaps you don't think that. Let us see on the basis of what Sonja said to you that you should not come.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a translation of this document, so could it please be called up. We've been waiting for almost one hour to have it uploaded, and if that's not possible, could it please be placed on the ELMO, the translation. We do have the translation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the State Security Service, and they caught sight of you already in January. And they are reporting that they noticed that you visited trouble spots and that they did not understand all of your activities as journalism, but as you said a moment ago, journalists were often considered to be spies. So could you please take a look at this text.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Could you make it clearer somehow? It's hard to -- there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am not accusing you. I am just indicating what it was that my daughter relied on when she denied access. It didn't -- it wasn't made up by herself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Cool.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, someone might praise you for your work, but our State Security Service was quite alarmed, saying that your activities should be followed as they may have an impact on the ability of the country to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2088, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D5122. 05122. The translation has not arrived yet. I just wanted to present the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It also comes from the state security sector, from Banja Luka, whereas the previous document was authored by the chief of state security. From the Krajina, they seem to be reporting that Robert Block, a journalist working for "The Independent," as well as Frank Westerman and Adrian Brown of the BBC, have crossed the border near Gradiska, entering the Republika Srpska in order to visit a 1st Corps press centre. According to our sources, the aforementioned journalists, after visiting the press centre and on his recommendation, contacted the municipal president in Banja Luka and Louis Gentille, UNHCR mission head, and so on and so forth. Can we go on to the next page. Did you indeed cross the border between Croatia and Republika Srpska near Gradiska on the 23rd of January?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. I used every trick in the book to cross wherever I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Gentille apparently said that pressure was being put on the UNHCR delegation and that, in that context, a private shop, a kiosk, was demolished. Next, there is mention of you visiting a collection centre of Serbs who had fled from the former BiH in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yeah, it's possible. I don't -- I don't recall I -- I'd be more comfortable seeing the translation, but from what I gather, yeah, it sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last page, please. I'll read it out. The chief of the CSB centre in Banja Luka says as follows, I quote: "The problem of entry of foreign journalists in Republika Srpska along the described lines has been going on for a while and we have informed you about that on a number of occasions but have not received any information from you. We again stress and believe that due to a timely approach to this problem, these categories of aliens should be addressed by the ministries involved in terms of a position that needs to be taken." Do you agree that it seems there was quite some correspondence about your presence there and that the state service deemed you to be overly active, especially in military issues and that it was not the assessment of the press centre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: There was a war. Of course I was very active in military issues. It was what I was covering. And, yeah, I -- I like to think that I was overly active, and I tended over the years to get under the skin of intelligence agencies of several governments for my reporting. I wear it as badge of honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May it be admitted and marked for identification pending translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification as D2089, but in the meantime, Mr. Karadzic, it's about time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show just one last document, which is 1D05123, relating to the same topic. It is dated the 10th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it seems you were watched and your movements observed daily, basically from one hour to the next; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I would think your security services were not doing their job if they were not doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the last page where it says -- this need not be broadcast. I need to protect the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Reference is made to your encounter with Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic who complained to the fact that journalists are being granted access to Republika Srpska without any prior screening or selection and then sent to him to be interviewed. He complained that the behaviour of certain representatives of this institution involved was unfair and he asked of them and of the RS government that the status -- their status be resolved in view of their rights. He also complained that there were annual secret reports published by that institution and that you and Frank Westerman gained insight into it. Do you agree that indeed you were in contact with the institution whose abbreviation you can see in the third paragraph? The fourth paragraph, the second line, you see the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I don't know who that organisation is. I mean, if the implication is that I was in contact with foreign intelligence forces and was acting on their behalf, it's complete nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Finish -- could the Chamber move into private session? Without translation, it's very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were familiar with the work of the UNHCR and the objections the VRS had, in particular by Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic about journalists and the UNHCR being one-sided. Were you able to hear such objections?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Oh, all the time. It was the daily -- daily accusations were made against foreign journalists by and large, particularly from America and Britain, and some from other countries, as well as the HCR, is that we were anti-Serb or pro-Muslim or pro-Croatian. You know, it's something that -- it just became the background noise of the conflict. I ignored it and did my job and figured as long as I was getting things accurate and trying to, you know, turn the same level of attention on every side, then I -- I was doing my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last topic, Mr. Block. You were able to observe that in Bijeljina, in RS, there was Janja and then there was Bosanski Kobas and Dubocac, many Muslim villages that remained untouched in Republika Srpska. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: There were times that it was always unusual to see that there were villages that for a while were -- some were allowed to exist for a certain period of time and were later be -- would later be emptied or a mosque would later be removed and that would cause people to want to leave, but, yeah, there were areas in which Muslims -- Muslims lived. They were there. They were nervous. It was -- you know, you can understand why, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were dozens of villages which remained untouched and lived in peace until the end of the war? And on the other hand, have you heard of a single Serb village in the federation which managed to remain untouched until September 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I -- I don't know the answer. Yes, I knew there were many villages where Muslims were -- I don't know what their pre-war population was and what it was by the end of the war. And in terms of Serb villages on the Muslim side, there were -- there were Serbs in cities that were under Bosnian control. Again, they weren't very happy or comfortable, just like they were -- just like the Muslims in the other villages. I don't know. I mean, certainly in the area around Srebrenica, the Serbian villages were -- were cleansed, but again, you know, it was a -- a messy situation, and it was not always easy to determine how things unfolded and at what time. There were times that we were shown villages, and often in the process of being shown villages it has a -- has an atmosphere of being a propaganda stunt. But, yes, there were -- there were exceptions to the rule on all sides, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Block. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark the last document as D2090. Mr. Mitchell, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Block, earlier today, at page 52, Mr. Karadzic asked you about his approval for Peter Arnett to go into Zepa and follow events there. And then at page 60 he asked you further questions about military restrictions on journalists and civilian restrictions on journalists and whether the civilian authorities were able to overcome that, and I just -- I have a couple of questions on this topic of restrictions of the movement of journalists and who was in control of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the first document I want to look at is 65 ter number 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is an order by the VRS Main Staff on 13 July 1995, signed by General Ratko Mladic, and I want to focus you in particular on paragraphs 4 and 5, which says: "In the area of combat operations in the wider areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, prevent the entry of all local and foreign journalists, except for the journalists of the VRS Main Staff Press Centre." And then paragraph 5: "Ban and prevent the giving of information, the making of announcements and statements to the media regarding the course, situation and results of combat operations in this area and the overall activities in this area, particularly on prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, escapees and similar." And my question regarding this document is very simple. Were you aware in July 1995 that General Mladic had specifically ordered that foreign journalists not be allowed into the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: No, I was not aware, but it was clear that there were no foreign journalists there. So one could only assume that it would have been by a -- by a -- someone senior in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Today at page 25 -- page 75 of the transcript, Mr. Karadzic read to you part of Dragan Cicic's article in which he said: "Few journalists who did get permits to go to Pale after the Serbs had conquered Srebrenica were explicitly told that they could take the road via Visegrad only, and it was quite impossible to get to the region of Srebrenica and Bratunac by this road." Now, I want to show you one more document related to the movements of journalists to Pale on 16 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you mean to tender that document, Mr. Mitchell, the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I would like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness didn't confirm anything about the document, so we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not confirm to a certain extent? He confirmed that there were no foreign journalists, and then was it not relevant to -- to his context?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's relevant. There's no question about that, but whether there was an order from the VRS that prevented foreign journalists from coming to that area is something that he himself didn't know, so I don't think it should be admitted by way of a document like this. But it's definitely relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you do not challenge the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there's sufficient foundation for admitting it through this witness. He's confirmed even though he wasn't specifically aware that there was a ban in place, he can certainly testify about the effect of that ban and has done so, so I think that gives sufficient basis for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree with you, Mr. Mitchell. This will be admitted as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Block, with that statement of Dragan Cicic in mind, that a few journalists were allowed in but explicitly told that they could take the road via Visegrad only, I want to show you one more document, which is 65 ter 7981.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. Could Mr. Mitchell also show us paragraph 2 where the route is mentioned, and it was the army who came up with that route to go through Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What document are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're just about to get to who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: JUDGE KWON: -- authorised the route of that troop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can see here this is another document of the VRS Main Staff dated 16 July. And it says that it's sent to the command of the 1st Podrinje and the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and the Drina Corps. Before I ask you a question, Mr. Block, do you know where Dobrun is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I need to see on a map. I'm not sure what you're getting at. It was in the middle of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking is that the -- the same route that Dragan Cicic was talking about, the Pale-Dobrun route? We can bring up a map if that would assist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: Yeah, that would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we could go to, perhaps, 65 ter 23519.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is misinterpretation. It is not the same route. This was the shortest route to Pale and not to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I can avoid the map if Mr. Karadzic agrees that the route via Dobrun is the crossing at Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, but that was the shortest way from Serbia to Pale and had nothing to do with Srebrenica or with the order for that matter. I simply allowed CNN to go to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
