utterances.text: I'll carry on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can see in the first paragraph here, Mr. Block, it says: "We hereby inform you that pursuant to an oral order by the president of the RS, the VRS has approved movement of a team [sic] of journalists from the following television stations: CNN (nine members) and David Paradine television (7 members), on the route Dobrun-Pale on," and that's a translation error. It should be 17 July 1995. You can see further down it says that: "Stopping, the filming of military facilities, and taking statements from members of the army is not permitted while travelling on this route -- travelling by this route." My question for you on this document, Mr. Block, is: In your experience going to Bosnia during the war, was it usual for Mr. Karadzic to get personally involved in approving the movement of journalists and what route they would travel on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT JEFFREY BLOCK
utterances.text: I certainly had to experience of it and I was unaware. However, everybody in a position of power had their favourite journalists and they were -- they did things for them when they felt it necessary for whatever particular interest they had to do that, but by and large, in this particular time, I mean, it was -- I had no knowledge of this and I don't recall a precedent myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Block. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you withdraw your question whether this Dobrun-Pale route was what Mr. Cicic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe Mr. Karadzic agreed that this was the same route when I said if I can avoid -- one second. I said I can avoid the map if Mr. Karadzic agrees that the route via Dobrun is the crossing at Visegrad. And he said yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he agreed with what you suggested, i.e., that's the route what Mr. Cicic was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I misunderstood. That's what I understood, Mr. President, that the crossing at Dobrun is at Visegrad. And we can bring up a map to confirm that, if it would assist, or unless Mr. Karadzic agrees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I agree it was the shortest route between Serbia and Pale, but it had nothing to do with Srebrenica and Bratunac. There were other border crossings there at Skelani, Ljubovija, and Zvornik. If one were to go to Pale, they would go through Visegrad, which had nothing to do with Srebrenica. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, unless my colleagues have questions for you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like to return to the issue of his notes, and I wonder if you would hear me outside of his presence on that before he's excused, or if you would prefer to deal with it in writing and make some order later, we can do that, but it might be useful to resolve it while he's still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to ask him to stay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea because I'm going to ask you to order him to turn over those notes, so it would be easier if he was still here if you were inclined to make that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he confirm that he made notes at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we referring to the Pirocanac interview? I'm not being inconvenient here, but I really do not believe I made notes because it wasn't an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, well, my request would be then if Mr. Block would look through his notebooks for that time period, and if he discovers the -- any notes concerning his contact on the 18th of July with Mr. Pirocanac, that he notify the Trial Chamber, and if that's the case -- or if he's -- if he says that they don't exist, if he could notify us of that and we can deal with it at that time if that's what he prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Mitchell, on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, just very briefly. I don't think that the issue of notes in any way changes your decision to admit Mr. Block's evidence on this specific conversation with Zoran Petrovic. Obviously Mr. Karadzic is looking to establish that his name doesn't appear in these notes, if there are any such notes, but even if that were the case, I would submit that that doesn't in any way undermine the veracity of his recollection of what Mr. Pirocanac says. So even if there are notes and even if they show what Dr. Karadzic wants them to show, that doesn't undermine or affect the admissibility of Mr. Block's oral testimony. So in these circumstances, I suggest it cannot be in the interests of justice to use the coercive power of the Chamber to turn over notes about a meeting and a conversation which Mr. Block has testified about from his recollection and which won't be undermined even if there is such notes and the absence of any reference in those notes. The last point I'd like to make is at best, even if Mr. Block found the notes, there's no reference to Mr. Karadzic, that would be a matter that went to the weight of his oral testimony in a very minor way, but at least fundamentally isn't an issue of the admissibility of his oral testimony as Mr. Robinson suggested earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I briefly reply. First of all, I'm just asking -- I'm not speaking about admissibility now. I'm just asking you to order him to look for the notes, but this particular issue, we have to be at the absolute height of vigilance. This goes directly to Dr. Karadzic's own mens rea and responsibility for this crime. If -- if this is in fact -- if what this witness says is relied on by the Chamber, it can have serious implications for your findings and your judgement in this case. And we hear very, very little evidence about Dr. Karadzic's personal involvement to do with anything to do with Srebrenica, and when we hear that evidence, we need to put you in a position where whatever decision you can make can be absolutely safe and absolutely correct. This is a very controversial piece of evidence. Triple hearsay to begin with. Now we're asking you to try to verify, to do everything you can to try to verify whether or not this is the kind of evidence you should rely on in your judgement. And maybe it's inconvenient to have Mr. Block go through his notebooks and look and see if he has a record of that conversation, but that's the very least that he can do in pursuit of justice and the very least that you can order if it's necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Block, can I ask you whether you are minded to voluntarily co-operate with the Defence so as to look into whether such notes exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the point of view of a journalist and someone in my profession, it's a slippery slope what you're asking for. It's -- just as we believe that when you go into naming sources, this is something that we can't do, to some degree I believe this same precedence extends to a journalist's notes which are notes for him or herself either as a mnemonic or to create observations that may have relevance at the time. But it is the actual article itself that is put together that is what stands and what ultimately is where we -- I am here to do in some ways, is to be in service of the articles that I presented. Insofar as it comes to my recollection of the conversations with -- with Zoran Petrovic in those days, number one, I do not believe I took notes on those days because there was really nothing to take notes about. We wanted to know what happened to the film and if copies existed and what he did. And as I said in my testimony, this was not something I put any journalistic resources towards. I don't know what the definition of contempt of court in this particular venue is, but I would find it very, very difficult to do. I would have no problems in looking into my notes as mnemonic to try to remember things before testimony, but being compelled to look into my notes for something that is really in many ways outside of the purview of my reporting, and as such and as we discussed in the -- in my interview with the Defence, this was in many ways at the level of hearsay, and I would not disagree with that. So I do not see the point of it, and I really think that asking me to do so does put in danger what I am trying to do today, which is basically find a way in which foreign correspondents, particularly American foreign correspondents, can feel comfortable in co-operating with a body like this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider the issue at later stage. I thank you again -- and for your coming to The Hague to give it. We appreciate it very much. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before the next witness is brought in if I could just raise one other issue that Dr. Karadzic has asked me to mention to the Trial Chamber and that is of concern to him and to his Defence team. And that is that one of the witnesses who testified for the Prosecution a few weeks ago, Mira Mihajlovic, who works in Sarajevo, has been the subject of news media articles in which the news media in Sarajevo has been calling for her removal in her current position because she gave testimony favourable to Dr. Karadzic concerning his character. And Dr. Karadzic is concerned, given the fact that we want to call a number of witnesses in our case during the Defence case, that this kind of issue can have a chilling effect on the willingness of people to testify on his behalf. So I'm not asking the Chamber to do anything at this point, I just want to bring it to your attention, and in the future if it appears to be something that's more of a problem, we will maybe ask the Chamber to take some action. But Dr. Karadzic asked me to bring this to your attention and I'm doing that now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Good afternoon, Ms. West. Your next witness is Mr. Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it he is on his way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth, so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Milan Lesic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where were your born?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Cazin, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you move to Canada?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why did you move to Canada?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: I escaped from former Yugoslavia and went to Austria. From Austria I emigrate to Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was there a reason that you left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: It was. I was young and I didn't like the Communist regime.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: I'm self-employed. I'm a developer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in 1993, were you a founding member of a Canadian charitable organisation called the Serbian Humanitarian Public Organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what prompted you to organise it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Well, the war start over there in 1991, 1992, beginning 1992, so we got together in Hamilton and Toronto and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to get closer to the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. 1992, we got together, and a bunch of us, we talked about what was going on in our old country. Then we got together again and organised, fill some applications, and we got registered as a humanitarian -- humanitarian Srpska Republika organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were part of your activities to raise funds?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we raised the funds to help the needy, like delivered some stuff to the Red Cross and to other people what is needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And besides the Red Cross, who were the intended recipients of your aid?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Whatever our committee delegate in Canada, they give us a letter, and myself I went many times and we took some -- took some samples in suitcases and we took some money and we helped -- helped the people that is needed. And then when we got over there, suggestion was made where should we give that help. So we split two way hospitals and three ways in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's back up for a moment. The recipients of your aid, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Ethnicity what that word -- needy? Or ethnicity, what does that word mean? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were they -- I'll give you an example. Were they Muslim, Croatian, were they Serbian? Were they --

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Oh, they were Serbians, all the Serbians. Everybody help their own. The Serbians help Serbians and other people help themselves -- their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And are you Serbian, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As part of your involvement in the organisation, did you -- there you go. Did you go to the area several times starting in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went approximately ten times over there from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And before your first trip in 1992, had you made any prior arrangements to meet anybody in regard to the aid that you wanted to distribute?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We just went there and got to Belgrade and got to Bosnian house and we talked over there. We meet some people and bishop, and they transport us over with helicopter to the Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's back up. Was your first trip in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was first trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And to where did you fly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: We flew from Toronto to Sofia, I believe, and from Sofia we were picked up by cars to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And with whom did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: I went with Ned Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you got to Belgrade, where was the first place you went?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: We went to that called Bosnian house, therefore Bosanska Vila, what they say. And there we met bishop from Chicago which we know, so we travelled with bishop to the Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how did you get from Belgrade to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: By helicopter, army helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know who arranged that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: I presume was Peter Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why do you presume that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Well, I was told later somebody had to arrange for us, also the bishop went with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now you mentioned that you went over approximately ten times?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you went over, did you take with you a camera and a video camera as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did take my Sony camera to take some pictures and the movies when we were giving -- giving aids from our humanitarian organisation from Toronto so that I can come back and show the group that money went in proper place and got the proper -- it went to proper hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So were you using the video footage and the cameras to show that you actually gave the money?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in August of 2009. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during that interview, did you give four video-tapes and several photos to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: I was ordered by the court in Canada to bring all the tapes, all the pictures, all my passports and everything, to give it to them everything that I had since 1992 to -- to present, to 1999 -- to 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you did that, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: And I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And that included four video-tapes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to December of 1992 when you got in the helicopter and you went to Pale. When you arrived in Pale, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: We went to -- it was Assembly held there and we were sitting and waiting and we had some -- I don't know what we had, some coffee or entertainment. And then we waited for Assembly so the bishop introduce us and we gave our money that we brought for the government, for the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have P01364.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now you said you were waiting for the Assembly. Did you actually attend an Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we attend. I was in the back, sitting in the back, Ned and I myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. We're going to show you some minutes from an Assembly session. This is dated 17 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May have page 77 of the English and which is corresponding to page 71 of the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lesic, this is something I showed you the other day so I know you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the middle paragraph towards the end, this is Ned Krajisnik speaking. Can you tell us who Ned is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Ned Krajisnik is -- that I know since 1972. He lives in Kitchener, and I live in other city, in Guelph.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And is he somebody who helped you put together this organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a member with us. He was the president of the committee and was another president, Ranko Rakanovic. And I was assistant treasurer from beginning, and after I was a treasurer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So here we see that Mr. Krajisnik is addressing the Assembly, and we won't read the whole paragraph, but he's talking about your organisation and how you put it together. And in this middle paragraph he actually says: "My colleague here, Milan Lesic, as the Most Reverend Metropolitan said, is, thank God, a quite rich man. He is rich because he worked hard and took good care of his money." And then the next paragraph, which started with "we decided," he said: "We decided to come here, to help as much as we can. Mr. Milan Lesic delivered $15.000 here for the media and propaganda, for I think that we have lost the war the most in that area. And our enemies have been the most successful on that account." Sir, you were present for this speech, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when Mr. -- when your friend Ned mentions media and propaganda, can you tell us about the concern that existed regarding the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of us Serbians in Canada, we -- we seen that we are lacking in a media publicity and all that. The media was quite biased, it was all other side and wasn't with us so we thought we need some help and get some support, and that's what we did, to get media to be at least in the middle ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And your concern in regard to media, is that something that you discussed with the people that you met in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I discussed with them and they agreed with me at that time and we also have a same agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So that concern you had was shared by the people you met in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was -- was the concern that the media was anti-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: That's how we felt. It was -- everything went against the Serb -- Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you have any discussions on this date or any dates thereafter with General Mladic or Mr. Karadzic regarding this issue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Well, after we handed our help that we brought, we went to the some room and we had drinks and talked. We talked about the media, how can we help and all that. We had some media person at that time, and President Karadzic says yes, media is -- is we are -- we need to improve on it. So did General Mladic. And we agreed with them and Biljana Plavsic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in Canada, what was the source of your information coming out of the region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: When we watched CNN, we always sees the lady by name Amanpour always against Serbs and against Serbs, Serbs did this, Serbs did that, Serbs did everything, and I couldn't believe it that we were so painted that way. So we went over and talked to the officials, like our people there, General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik, Momcilo Krajisnik, and all of us, what's going on. So they say is all the lies and that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as I understand it, then part of the source of your information from the media was from CNN. Did you also get media reports from stations in the region?

utterances.speaker: MILAN LESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did but very short, but we did -- what I did personally, at my house we installed a dish 1992, before war began, and then that dish would bring all the news from over there immediately and that helped us knowing what was going on in -- in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to move to a different subject. Might this be a good time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll call it a day. We'll continue tomorrow, Mr. Lesic, at 9.00. In the meantime, you might have heard about this, but you are not to discuss about your testimony with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
